These activities will assist local farmers, ranchers, and value-added producers, in growing their businesses to meet the needs of the local food system, and subsequently build food self-sufficiency and economic resiliency for the isolated and vulnerable island of Kauaʻi.
updated_description: Mālama Kauaʻi will launch the Moloaʻa ʻĀINA Center food hub by Fall 2023, a key initiative designed to bolster Kauaʻi’s local agriculture industry and enhance food self-sufficiency for the island’s residents. This project will fund critical staff positions essential for expanding programs and services associated with the new facility, which includes the construction and equipping of a central location for food processing, storage, and business assistance. The anticipated outcomes of this work include a projected 10% increase in average yearly sales for over 175 local farmers and food producers, with 60% of these businesses being small operations. Furthermore, at least 25 members of the Moloaʻa Irrigation Cooperative will utilize the facility for value-added product production. This project will directly benefit Kauaʻi’s farmers, ranchers, and food processors, enabling them to meet the demands of the local food system and increase their operational scale. The intended beneficiaries include the island’s residents who will gain access to a more robust and reliable local food supply. Ultimately, this work aims to strengthen the overall resilience of Kauaʻi’s agricultural sector, providing greater economic stability for those involved and ensuring a more secure food source for the community.

awardee_name: Maine Dayboat Scallops Inc (aka Downeast Dayboat)
original_description:
Dayboat Blue will increase consumption of Maine seafood with a new distribution method combining the ease of online ordering with the lower environmental costs, increased connections and better prices of CSA-style local pickups.
Modeled after the British Columbia-based Skipper Otto program, Dayboat Blue will align with retail partners in 3 northeastern locations to promote and optimize seafood pick up events. Customers will order Maine seafood online and collect it at a local retail partner. Storage information, recipes and videos will be available via QR codes to reduce packaging materials. Initial pickups will serve as a model for expansion to other communities.
Thermal shipping materials and air transportation represent  significant costs that would be better allocated as higher producer prices, lower consumer prices and enhanced education and promotion. Dayboat Blue will pay producers higher prices while offering consumers convenient, well-priced premium local seafood along with the tools they need (videos, recipes, online interactive cooking events and Q&A sessions) to increase their comfort level with at-home preparation, which will help increase purcha ses.
Additional foot traffic of motivated food buyers will benefit pickup partners. We will all benefit from less packaging and air transport.
Downeast Dayboat will serve as lead organization with founder Togue Brawn as lead promoter and Jocelyn Gabriel as project coordinat or. Kelly Tinkler of Purechalk Marketing will act as the project manager and will oversee all aspects of the project . Subawards will be awarded to food consultant Johanna Kolodny, nutritionist Kristy Del Coro, a video production company and a photographer..
updated_description: Dayboat Blue will increase the consumption of Maine seafood by establishing a new distribution model combining online ordering with CSA-style local pickup events, modeled after the British Columbia-based Skipper Otto program. This project will align with retail partners in three northeastern locations to promote and optimize seafood pickup events, offering consumers convenient access to premium, locally sourced seafood. The project anticipates increasing sales for Maine seafood producers while simultaneously providing consumers with the tools necessary to confidently prepare seafood at home, including QR codes linking to recipe videos and interactive cooking events. Dayboat Blue will pay producers higher prices, reducing reliance on thermal shipping materials and air transportation, and will focus on streamlining operations to reduce packaging and transportation costs. The intended outcome is to bolster sales for seafood processors and farmers, and to increase consumer interest in purchasing Maine seafood. The beneficiaries of this project include seafood producers, retail partners, and ultimately, consumers seeking high-quality, locally produced food. Retail partners will benefit from increased foot traffic and sales opportunities. Dayboat Blue, led by Togue Brawn and Jocelyn Gabriel, will engage a food consultant, a nutritionist, a video production company, and a photographer to support the initiative, ensuring the project’s effective implementation and operation.

original_description: This project will enable Freshlist to expand the market for local and regional foods in one of the fastest growing metropolitan areas in the US. Freshlist’s hub currently faces limited infrastructure and organizational capacity, which hinders their ability to capitalize on both direct-to-consumer and wholesale market opportunities for their network of 115 farmers and 39 value-added producers. To address these challenges, Freshlist will lease a refrigerated vehicle and additional warehouse space to increase aggregation, storage, and distribution capacity, hire staff dedicated to growing, managing, and executing Freshlist's direct-to-consumer home delivery business, collaborate with a regional food hub partner to expand the availability and selection of local foods, develop effective marketing strategies to promote local foods, and enhance existing technology systems.
updated_description: Freshlist will undertake a project to expand the market for local and regional foods within a rapidly growing metropolitan area, capitalizing on opportunities for both direct-to-consumer and wholesale sales. This initiative will involve several key elements, including the lease of a refrigerated vehicle and additional warehouse space to significantly increase aggregation, storage, and distribution capacity for the network’s 115 farmers and 39 value-added producers. The project anticipates expanding access to locally produced goods for consumers and supporting the operations of farmers and ranchers. The expected outcome is a bolstered Freshlist hub, capable of efficiently managing the increased volume of products and facilitating broader market reach. The project aims to strengthen the position of stakeholders involved in the local food system. By expanding Freshlist’s capabilities, the project seeks to increase the availability of goods produced by these farmers and processors to a wider customer base. Freshlist will collaborate with a regional food hub partner to broaden the selection and enhance the overall supply chain, ultimately improving the flow of goods from producers to consumers. This expansion will positively impact the food system by creating greater demand for regionally sourced agricultural products.

original_description: Good Stuff will lower barriers for local producers becoming marketplace-ready with their local valueadded agricultural products by training them on capacity-building specialty kitchen equipment and by providing resources and networking to build mutually beneficial connections with local producers. Good Stuff will hire a dedicated Market Access Coordinator, expand the incubator kitchen capacity for valueadded production, develop a resource guide and outreach plan (market events, social media, networking events) to increase access to information and market access points, and limit food waste through efficient processing. Project outcomes are expected to include marketplace-ready producers with locally sourced value-added agricultural products for sale, increased wholesale opportunities for producers and farmers, and increased capacity for processing local produce for value-added production.
updated_description: Good Stuff will facilitate market readiness for local agricultural producers by providing specialized kitchen equipment and resources, alongside strategic networking opportunities to cultivate mutually beneficial relationships with other producers and stakeholders. The project will encompass expanding the capacity of an incubator kitchen facility for value-added production and the development of a comprehensive resource guide and outreach plan, utilizing market events and social media to increase access to information and market access points. This initiative aims to minimize food waste through efficient processing methods, ultimately leading to the creation of marketplace-ready producers with locally sourced value-added agricultural products available for sale. Anticipated outcomes include increased wholesale opportunities for farmers and ranchers, alongside a significant rise in the capacity for local produce processing, benefiting all involved. The primary beneficiaries of Good Stuff’s efforts will be farmers, ranchers, and processors, as well as the consumers seeking access to fresh, locally produced goods. By streamlining the application process for prescribed activities, Good Stuff seeks to create a system that fosters the growth of local food businesses and expands access to regional agricultural products for sale. This project directly supports the development of a more robust and accessible local food system, concentrating on practical solutions for production and distribution.

original_description: Food hubs are an integral part of the food system as they reduce burden on farmers to market their products and make it easier for buyers to source locally from multiple producers. However, many small farmers in Western New York are not able to sell to a food hub because they do not meet minimum case numbers or other requirements. Similarly, many small buyers seeking to source local, like nonprofits serving low resource communities, small stores, and restaurants may not have access to a food hub due to minimum orders, cost-prohibitive mark-ups, or other barriers. There is a need for streamlined food aggregation and distribution for small farmers and buyers. FreshFix currently aggregates locally grown produce for  home delivery to  retail customers and has seen increasing demand to  also offer wholesale to  nonprofit organizations  and small food businesses .  For this project, we propose expanding operations to include wholesale and creating a hybrid food hub model that will fill a gap in small-scale local food aggregation  in our region. To ensure success, we will train and provide supplies to  farmers and coordinate a campaign to promote locally grown food to consumers . We will work with partners including the University at Buffalo to provide evaluation, partnership development,  campaign tracking, and technical assistance to  nonprofits on developing food insecurity programming; and the Massachusetts Avenue Project to recruit entrepreneurs to create value-added products using excess produce and reduce farm waste. We will also collaborate with an advisory group of farmers and community partners.
updated_description: FreshFix proposes a project to establish a hybrid food hub model designed to streamline food aggregation and distribution for small farmers and buyers within Western New York. This initiative will address the existing barriers faced by many small farmers who do not meet the requirements of traditional food hubs, as well as buyers such as nonprofits serving low-resource communities, small stores, and restaurants. The project will involve the purchase of supplies to support farmers in aggregating locally grown produce, alongside the creation of a campaign to promote locally grown food to consumers. Anticipated outcomes include increased access to regionally produced agricultural products, strengthened relationships between farmers and buyers, and reduced farm waste through the development of value-added products by entrepreneurs. The primary beneficiaries of this project will be farmers seeking new markets for their goods, as well as consumers seeking fresh, locally sourced food. Furthermore, the project aims to assist nonprofits in developing food insecurity programming and support entrepreneurs in creating value-added products utilizing excess produce. This initiative will also engage a collaborative advisory group of farmers and community partners to ensure the long-term success and sustainability of the food hub model, ultimately contributing to a more efficient and accessible local food system.

original_description:
The Community and Commerce: Cultivating Market Capacity through Peer Exchange project, facilitated by the Appalachian Center for Economic Networks (ACEnet) will manage a peer learning network to identify and catalogue successful models of community markets rooted in local ownership. These market champions in Ohio and West Virginia, have activated local food economies to design inclusive, community marketplaces that layer cooperative values, social enterprise practices and explicit value chain coordination. Established and emergent markets will serve as learning centers: Local Roots Market & Café, Keller Market House, The Wild Ramp, Mountain Farm Community Grocery, and The Public Market. The four established marketplaces, currently source from over 300 produce farmers, livestock operators and value-added processors, enabling many local vendors the first entry point in selling at a wholesale level. Project activities will address challenges the food enterprise market face in expanding  vendors; managing ordering and procurement systems; and innovating marketing and branding strategies. 
 
As project lead, ACEnet will convene monthly zoom calls, schedule site visits with the host food enterprises participating as learning centers, and conduct research to identify resources and address gaps for producers, market managers and resource providers. Projects outputs will include: seven site visits and cohort convenings, a market replication guide for market expansion, vendor management and recruitment, customer promotions and market plans, and multimedia training materials such as webinars, workshops, short videos, and podcasts open to the larger network of food economy practitioners.
updated_description: The Appalachian Center for Economic Networks (ACEnet) will manage a peer learning network to identify and catalogue successful models of community markets rooted in local ownership, focusing on activating local food economies through inclusive marketplaces. This project will support the expansion of existing community markets – Local Roots Market & Café, Keller Market House, The Wild Ramp, Mountain Farm Community Grocery, and The Public Market – which currently source from over 300 farmers, ranchers, and value-added processors, providing a critical first entry point for many local vendors to engage in wholesale sales. The anticipated outcomes of this project include the development of a market replication guide to facilitate the expansion of these successful marketplaces, coupled with support for vendor management and recruitment strategies, and the creation of customer promotions and comprehensive market plans. original_description:
The Main Idea
Play. Advocate. Live Well.’s (PAL) ’s project will strengthen and expand the Food Hub’s capacity to serve more people in Spartanburg County, South Carolina, and provide increased economic opportunities for producers and food businesses in the region.

The Issue
Although agribusiness is the largest economic sector in South Carolina, farms in Spartanburg County, and some of its neighboring counties, are losing money. All the while, grocery store shelves remain sporadically stocked following the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, highly processed, cheap food is abundant, and access to fresh, local healthy food is very limited. Fresh, local food volume and infrastructure for local food need to be increased.

The Vision
In partnership with multiple organizations including Ruth’s Gleanings, Hub City Farmers Market, Carolina Farm Stewardship Association, and Spartanburg County Farm Bureau, and led by a Food Hub Committee that includes a farmer, a person with lived experience, and many others, PAL will grow and strengthen their food hub to create more opportunity for residents and institutions to access local food. Food will be purchased and donated to underserved communities and sold to restaurants, stores, schools, and hospitals. Trainings for producers will be offered. An “Eat Local” campaign will be launched. At the same time, sustainability will be sought for local food system work by advocating for regular funding through the state legislature.
updated_description: Play. Advocate. Live Well.’s (PAL) project aims to strengthen and expand the Food Hub’s capacity to serve more people in Spartanburg County, South Carolina, and to provide increased economic opportunities for farmers and food businesses within the region. Anticipated outcomes include expanded access to locally produced food for consumers and institutions, such as restaurants, stores, schools, and hospitals, and the creation of more viable markets for farmers and ranchers. The project will support the increased production and distribution of agricultural products, addressing the sporadic availability of fresh food currently observed on grocery store shelves. PAL will work in partnership with organizations like Ruth’s Gleanings, Hub City Farmers Market, Carolina Farm Stewardship Association, and Spartanburg County Farm Bureau to facilitate the flow of goods from producers to end-users. The Food Hub Committee, comprised of individuals with various perspectives, will guide the project’s direction. The project seeks to create a sustainable local food system by advocating for consistent state legislative funding. Ultimately, the project will benefit farmers, ranchers, processors, and other stakeholders involved in the local food supply chain, contributing to a more robust and accessible food system within Spartanburg County.

original_description:
Despite high-value crops and proximity to major Bay Area food markets, agriculture has been in decline in San Mateo County (SMC), California, for decades. Local producers, most of whom run small operations, face a host of challenges: transportation and distribution barriers due to coastal locations, ineffectively tapping into local markets, and lack of nearby processing facilities. Through recent collaborative efforts, local producers identified the need for a food hub to revitalize the San Mateo County farming and ranching industries. This planning project will continue the community-designed development of a food hub to improve the viability of local farming operations by expanding markets and improving aggregation and distribution opportunities.
Objectives include: 1) Assess the needs of local small farms and ranches; and 2) Design a business plan for a food hub that will provide services and opportunities to improve the viability of local farms and ranches. The main project outcome will be a published business plan that has been driven and informed by the community at each stage of development. Project beneficiaries are SMC farmers and ranchers. This planning process will focus on historically underserved producers, including new/beginning farmers and those from underrepresented communities, including female, and BIPOC producers. The San Mateo Resource Conservation District will lead the project. Brisa Ranch, and local nonprofits TomKat Ranch Educational Foundation, and Kitchen Table Advisors will receive subawards to collaborate on project activities.
updated_description: San Mateo Resource Conservation District is undertaking a planning project to revitalize agriculture in San Mateo County (SMC), California, addressing a long-standing decline in local farming and ranching operations despite the region’s high-value crops and proximity to major food markets. The primary outcome of this project is a detailed business plan, collaboratively developed with input from the SMC farming and ranching community, which will guide the food hub’s operations and ensure it effectively meets the needs of its stakeholders. The anticipated results will improve the viability of local agricultural businesses and increase the availability of locally produced goods to consumers. The beneficiaries of this project are the farmers and ranchers within San Mateo County, as well as the broader network of food businesses and associated stakeholders involved in the regional food system. This planning process prioritizes support for historically marginalized producers. The San Mateo Resource Conservation District will lead this effort, partnering with Brisa Ranch, TomKat Ranch Educational Foundation, and Kitchen Table Advisors to ensure comprehensive community engagement and the development of a robust and sustainable food hub model.

original_description:
The Norton Regional Health Foundation (NRHF) requests an LFPP planning grant to design a correctional facility‐based farm‐to‐institution program to increase rural access to local, healthy food. This recommendation comes from a recently completed 2022 Regional Food System Assessment for Norton and surrounding counties in rural Northwest Kansas. The project will take place in the USDA Economic Research Service Low Access area (Tract #20137951700).
The Regional Food System Assessment highlighted the demand for more local food purchasing from the regional hospital and school district. To meet this demand, NRHF needed to identify a production partner able to produce needed items at scale. However, with a lack of specialty crop producers in Northwest Kansas, the Norton Correctional Facility was identified as a possible solution. They currently operate a 10‐acre fruit and vegetable farm, and have the capacity and interest in growing for local institutions.
This planning grant will be used to test the feasibility of developing a local institutional supply chain using produce grown at the correctional facility farm that supports workforce development in agriculture for residents of the facility.
NRHF will accomplish the following goals:
●	Complete a feasibility study to determine the possibility of establishing a farm‐to‐institution value chain based at the Norton Correctional Facility.
●	Create an agriculture and farm skill workforce development program for Norton Correctional Facility residents that can support them in finding jobs upon their release.
●	Build a corrections‐based farm‐to‐institution model that can be shared with other state correctional facilities.
updated_description: The Norton Regional Health Foundation (NRHF) is requesting a planning grant to design a correctional facility-based farm-to-institution program aimed at increasing access to local, healthy food for farmers and consumers in rural Northwest Kansas. This project will utilize the existing 10-acre fruit and vegetable farm operated at the Norton Correctional Facility, a location identified as a potential solution due to a lack of specialty crop producers in the region. The project’s goal is to establish a value chain that supports the hospital and school district’s needs for locally produced agricultural products. NRHF intends to conduct a feasibility study to determine the possibility of creating this farm-to-institution model, focusing on the production of items suitable for institutional consumption. The anticipated outcome is the development of a system where agricultural products grown at the correctional facility farm are directly supplied to local institutions. This would benefit stakeholders involved in the food supply chain, including the correctional facility residents, local farmers, and the regional hospital and school district. Ultimately, the project seeks to create a sustainable model that can be replicated in other state correctional facilities, supporting the availability of locally sourced food for consumers and contributing to a more localized food system.

The purpose of this project is to increase market opportunities for value‐added food businesses, and for the local farmers they source from.

original_description:
The Eastern Food Hub Collaborative (EFC), a program of Local Food Hub, is a network of food hubs and food system organizations working together to expand opportunities for farmers and equitable access to good food for all people. EFC includes 12 food hub members and five collaborating organizations, representing grower communities and food hub networks along a 1,000-mile stretch of the Eastern United States from Maine to South Carolina. In 2021, the food hub members of the Collaborative procured $18M+ in local food from 800+ participating producers, with collaborating organizations supporting efforts through local network management, value chain coordination, and grower services.
Through this program, the EFC will complete four planning objectives:
•	Obj1: Undertake a multi-year, multi-stakeholder strategic planning process to establish a five- year vision for equitable and impactful network development and governance.
•	Obj2: Respond to changing technology needs by piloting integrated supply/demand forecasting and production planning systems, as well as developing tools to increase collaboration on food system resilience, access, and equity.
•	Obj3: Design a hub-to-hub (H2H) trade agreement toolkit, providing best practices and financial proformas based on real-world transactions between members.
•	Obj4: Facilitate virtual and face-to-face convenings of EFC members and outside stakeholders, resulting in demonstrably increased peer-to-peer engagement, resource sharing, and trade.
During the program, the EFC will grow to support 1,200 growers with over $30M in procurement, provide new market opportunities for 20 food hub trading partners and 10 collaborating organizations, and generate $40M in gross sales of local and regional food.
updated_description: The Eastern Food Hub Collaborative (EFC) is undertaking a comprehensive program to expand opportunities for farmers and enhance equitable access to good food for all people across a 1,000-mile stretch of the Eastern United States. This initiative aims to procure over $30 million in local food annually from a projected 1,200 growers, supporting a network of 20 food hub trading partners and 10 collaborating organizations, ultimately generating $40 million in gross sales of local and regional food. The EFC will achieve this through four key objectives: developing a five-year strategic vision for network development and governance; piloting integrated supply/demand forecasting and production planning systems; designing a hub-to-hub trade agreement toolkit; and facilitating increased peer-to-peer engagement and resource sharing among EFC members and external stakeholders. The anticipated outcomes include the growth of regional food systems, creating new market access for farmers, ranchers, and processors, and bolstering the overall capacity of local food businesses. Specifically, the EFC will support a significant increase in the volume of local food being moved through the system, while simultaneously connecting producers with consumers seeking high-quality, regionally sourced products. The primary beneficiaries of this project will be the farmers and ranchers participating in the network, as well as the food hubs and processors involved in the supply chain, ultimately benefiting the communities that rely on access to fresh, local food.

CSA is a critical market for small‐scale farms in Oregon, particularly for beginning and BIPOC farmers with limited capital. Yet only 8% of the population knows of CSA, and only 1.5% participate1. Oregonians are known for buying local, being ecologically minded, and championing plant‐based diets. There is great potential to capture this untapped market through educating consumers about the benefits of local food consumption. This project will identify and address gaps between current and potential CSA consumers, increasing market opportunities for CSA farmers.

PNWCSA will contract with Bloom Communications, or similar research firm, to study the values and food purchasing behaviors of a diverse array of Oregonians, including residents with limited income and access to fresh food. Subsequently PNWCSA will work with Birch Social, a local marketing company rooted in the local food system, to develop a strategy to promote CSA to new consumers. PNWCSA and regional partners will then administer this campaign throughout the state.

As knowledge of our food system’s impact on the environment increases, so will consumer demand for sustainably grown food. This project supports small‐scale farmers by inspiring consumers to take part in Oregon’s vibrant local food system. With 125 farms in our coalition, 60% of them being new and beginning farmers, and 35% experiencing social discrimination, and with close relationships with local food organizations throughout the state, PNWCSA is poised to maximize the impact of a regional CSA marketing campaign.
updated_description: PNWCSA recognizes a significant opportunity to expand market access for small-scale farms in Oregon, particularly for beginning farmers and those with limited capital. This project will address a gap in consumer awareness regarding Community Supported Agriculture (CSA) models, aiming to increase participation and support for Oregon’s agricultural sector. Specifically, PNWCSA will partner with Bloom Communications, or a comparable research firm, to conduct a study of the values and food purchasing behaviors of a broad range of Oregon residents. Subsequently, PNWCSA will collaborate with Birch Social, a local marketing company, to develop and implement a regional marketing strategy designed to promote CSA to new consumers. Through this campaign, PNWCSA and its regional partners will actively engage with farmers and consumers throughout the state, increasing the visibility of CSA options. The anticipated outcome of this project is a measurable increase in consumer interest and participation within the CSA market, ultimately benefiting Oregon’s agricultural producers. This initiative will directly support the 125 farms within the PNWCSA coalition, including 60% of the farms that are new or beginning operations and 35% of which face challenges accessing markets. The primary beneficiaries of this project include the farmers and ranchers involved in the coalition, alongside the consumers who will gain access to locally sourced food. The project is designed to strengthen the entire agricultural value chain, connecting producers with the people who value their products.

original_description:
Regional berry crop production of elderberry, black currant, aronia, and honeyberry is a major economic opportunity for Midwest farmers and, as woody perennials, these crops can sequester carbon to reduce levels of greenhouse gasses in the atmosphere. Although active market demand is a primary limiting factor, preliminary stakeholder conversations suggest that tapping into the robust markets for small fruit is within reach. Turnkey funding will be used to fully research this opportunity in the Midwest and develop a berry marketing and branding campaign, with associated materials. The campaign will help all four crops collectively and individually – for example, harnessing existing consumer awareness around elderberries to elevate the positioning of others, including aronia, which could convert stranded aronia acreage from liability to asset.
The Savanna Institute, a Midwest agroforestry nonprofit, will develop a marketing strategy, plan, and materials to position the four berries as being desirable in the minds of Midwest buyers and consumers. The project will leverage our fruit and nut crop market development expertise, our regional and national network of farmers and food industry contacts, and a contract with Taste Profit Marketing, a specialty food business marketing and branding firm. Our networks will be invaluable not just for this market research and campaign development, but also for the next steps of funding and launching the campaign. A “Midwest Berry Marketing Board” or equivalent stakeholder-led structure to emerge from these efforts, and anticipate transferring to it the incubated assets (whether before or after the campaign launch).
updated_description: The Savanna Institute is undertaking a project to develop a berry marketing and branding campaign for elderberry, black currant, aronia, and honeyberry production within the Midwest region. This initiative will leverage turnkey funding to fully research the potential of these crops as a viable economic opportunity for farmers and processors, with the goal of tapping into existing demand for small fruits. The project will result in a comprehensive marketing strategy, detailed plans, and associated materials designed to position these berries favorably with Midwest buyers and consumers, potentially transforming stranded aronia acreage into a valuable asset. The Savanna Institute, in collaboration with Taste Profit Marketing, will utilize its established network of farmers and food industry contacts to facilitate this effort. The anticipated outcome is the establishment of a recognized brand identity for the four berry crops, increasing their market appeal and ultimately benefiting farmers and processors. The primary beneficiaries of this project include farmers cultivating these berries, as well as those involved in processing and distribution, seeking to expand their market reach and sales. This project aims to strengthen local food systems and bolster economic opportunities within the Midwest berry industry.

original_description: The Appalachian Producers Cooperative (APC) is the first farmer-owned cooperative established in Tennessee in over 50 years. APC is constructing a 16,000 square foot USDA-inspected meat processing facility, opening Jan. 2025, to serve farmers in 26 counties in Northeast Tennessee and Southwest Virginia. The facility will double the processing capacity in the region. APC will offer regional farmers fee-for-service processing and the opportunity to sell finished cattle under a cooperative owned brand of meat and value-added products. APC is working with local livestock farmers to develop a pipeline of finished cattle that are bred on a schedule and meet carcass quality standards. APC will hire a marketing director and marketing consulting firm and partner with Appalachian Resource Conservation and Development Council to conduct market research, develop its brand, implement a marketing campaign, and establish at least 30 accounts with wholesale buyers. The co-op branded sales will allow local farmers to access wholesale markets and serve the region's restaurants, grocery stores, and institutions at a scale individual farmers cannot serve. APC will partner with University of Tennessee Extension to provide technical assistance and education to producers to improve herd genetics, nutrition, and husbandry practices to supply 2,500 head of finished cattle to the cooperative annually. This project will benefit 1,200 family farms in Central Appalachia
updated_description: Appalachian Producers Cooperative is developing a significant project to establish a new USDA-inspected meat processing facility in Northeast Tennessee and Southwest Virginia, set to open in January 2025. This facility, encompassing 16,000 square feet, will dramatically increase processing capacity in the region, facilitating the cooperative’s mission to double the available processing volume. The co-op intends to offer fee-for-service processing to regional farmers, allowing them to sell finished cattle under a branded cooperative product line and develop a pipeline of approximately 2,500 head of finished cattle annually, sourced from 1,200 family farms. This initiative will support ranchers and processors, providing access to wholesale markets and enabling sales to restaurants, grocery stores, and institutions. The cooperative aims to establish at least 30 accounts with wholesale buyers, bolstering the economic viability of local farms. The project will support the development of a robust supply chain and enhance the ability of farmers to compete effectively within regional and national markets. The anticipated outcome is a strengthened local food system, benefiting farmers and consumers alike by increasing access to locally produced meat products.

original_description:
Rooted Farmers is a women-run online sales platform for small farms, built and led by a team of farmers.

We facilitate hyper-local distribution of agricultural products through our networked virtual marketplace, allowing farms to access, promote, and sell their inventory to an audience of local buyers. Initially launched in 2019 to support local flower sales, Rooted is now completing a multi-year project in partnership with the University of New Hampshire to expand our platform to support food hubs, specialty crop farms, and value-add producers across the US.
updated_description: Rooted Farmers is undertaking a multi-year project to expand its online sales platform, initially established in 2019, to support a wider range of agricultural businesses across the United States. The core purpose of this project is to facilitate the hyper-local distribution of agricultural products through a networked virtual marketplace, enabling small farms, ranchers, and value-add producers to access, promote, and sell their inventory directly to local consumers. This expansion will involve the development of infrastructure to accommodate a broader selection of food products, including those from specialty crop farms and businesses involved in processing. Rooted Farmers anticipates that this project will significantly increase the reach of participating farms, improving their ability to connect with local markets and enhance the availability of regionally produced goods. The anticipated outcomes include a strengthened supply chain for farmers and ranchers, a greater selection of goods accessible to consumers, and increased revenue streams for producers. The primary beneficiaries of this project encompass a wide range of stakeholders, including independent farmers, ranchers, food processors, and the consumers who value locally sourced agricultural products. Ultimately, Rooted Farmers aims to build a more robust and efficient system for distributing food within local communities, creating opportunities for economic growth and strengthening the connection between producers and their customers.

original_description:
Horse Shoe Ranch is a rapidly growing pastured poultry operation and distribution hub located on 100 acres outside
Pottstown, PA. Over the past three years, we have developed a robust aggregation and distribution system that allows us to
support other small and mid-size producers, hauling both their products and ours to markets at the same time. The 59
existing restaurants, retailers, and CSAs that work with us are able to efficiently consolidate orders from several vendors
into one coordinated delivery. There is strong demand from both producers and buyers to partner with our aggregation
network, but expansion has not been possible as our capacity is limited.
A start-up investment is needed to formalize and streamline operations, and appropriately staff the “Horse Shoe Hub”
outside of our own farm staff so that we can serve more farmers, expand our distribution geography, increase days of
delivery, and connect producers to new markets. LFPP grant funding will help us to 1) create systems for a formalized
"Horse Shoe Hub" distribution network that serves small and mid-size Pennsylvania producers; 2) launch the expanded
"Horse Shoe Hub" to connect local producers to regional markets; and 3) build a broad customer base of restaurants and
retailers in expanded geographies to create more market access for partner farms. This project will benefit 27 farmers, 40
retailers, and 80+ restaurants by the end of the project period.
updated_description: Horse Shoe Ranch is undertaking a project to formalize and expand its existing aggregation and distribution network, recognizing strong demand from farmers and buyers for its services. This project will involve the construction and operationalization of a dedicated “Horse Shoe Hub” facility, designed to streamline processes and increase capacity, and the development of formalized systems for managing the hub’s operations. The anticipated outcomes of this project include the ability to serve more Pennsylvania producers, expand the geographic reach of distribution, and increase the number of days of delivery services provided. Ultimately, Horse Shoe Ranch aims to connect a greater number of farmers to regional markets, securing increased market access for partner farms. By the end of the project period, the project is expected to benefit 27 farmers, 40 retailers, and 80+ restaurants, representing a significant expansion of the ranch’s impact on the local food system. This expanded network will provide crucial support to producers seeking to connect with consumers and businesses, offering a consolidated delivery solution and broader market opportunities. The project’s success relies on the creation of a more efficient and robust system for handling the volume of products moving through the distribution channel.

original_description:
Woodberry Kitchen has been sourcing exclusively from local producers since our launch in 2007. Over time, we identified a gap in the local Mid-Atlantic value chain: the need to align customer demand with the short harvest window. Farmers need to move excess produce, and consumers need simple ways to access local food year-round. Our solution is CanningShed, a value-added processor with exclusively local sourcing created by some of the most knowledgeable local food chefs in the region. CanningShed will build upon our existing relationships with regional producers, restaurants, groceries, and consumers. The initiative will operate in the middle of the supply chain, purchasing produce in large volumes from Mid-Atlantic farmers, and transforming that into desirable shelf-stable value-added products.

To achieve these goals, we will 1) Design a value-added product line that highlights the local riches of the Mid-Atlantic; 2) Build the marketing infrastructure needed to support CanningShed and promote partner farms, and 3) Launch CanningShed with a comprehensive marketing effort, connecting farmers, chefs, retailers, and consumers. By project’s end, we intend to produce 20 new value-added products, all with labels highlighting the producers from whom the ingredients are sourced. Products will be sold to at least 30 local and regional restaurants, groceries, and retailers, and promoted direct-to-consumer at local farmers markets.
updated_description: Woodberry Kitchen recognizes a critical need within the Mid-Atlantic food system to address the challenge of matching farmer production with consumer demand, particularly during short harvest windows. This project will establish CanningShed, a value-added processing operation utilizing exclusively local sourcing from regional producers, including farmers, ranchers, and processors, to transform large volumes of produce into shelf-stable products. CanningShed will build upon existing relationships and create a new intermediary role in the supply chain, focusing on developing a product line of 20 new items that prominently feature the origins of their ingredients, sourced from local producers. These products will be distributed to at least 30 local and regional restaurants, groceries, and retailers, and will be promoted directly to consumers via local farmers markets. The anticipated outcome is the creation of a robust system that supports farmers by providing a market outlet for their goods, while simultaneously offering consumers convenient access to fresh, locally produced food year-round. Ultimately, the project aims to benefit all stakeholders – farmers, processors, and consumers – by strengthening the local food economy and reducing food waste.

original_description:
The Local Inland Northwest Cooperative (LINC) has tested growth opportunities through its local farm to table subscription program (LINC Box), focusing on two key prospects for further development:
Increasing the variety of subscription shares, focusing on new small- and mid-sized farms and value-added producers.
Optimizing geographic reach and efficient routing of subscription deliveries.
These objectives will grow the economic viability of the LINC food hub and its producers, laying the groundwork for long-term expansion of year-round markets for producers and offering continuous consumer access to local foods.
Building upon the 74 producers currently benefiting from the LINC Box program, LINC will onboard 24 new producers including beginning farmers and undeserved producers, and add an additional 12 new value-added agricultural products as subscription items.
LINC will conduct market outreach, producer onboarding, and research to optimize year-round subscription offerings. Staff will assess routing efficiencies and partner with 9 businesses in the Inland Northwest Region to establish new distribution locations. LINC’s marketing team will work closely with key partners to increase consumer knowledge and purchasing of local agricultural products through these avenues.
Ultimately, these activities will enable market access breakthroughs for LINC and its producers, establishing long-term revenue streams and efficiency necessary for sustainable food chain coordination.
updated_description: The Local Inland Northwest Cooperative (LINC) is undertaking a strategic project to expand its local farm-to-table subscription program, LINC Box, with the primary purpose of enhancing the economic viability of the food hub and its participating producers. This initiative will involve the onboarding of 24 new producers, including beginning farmers and those involved in value-added agricultural products, alongside the addition of 12 new product offerings within the subscription boxes. LINC will also optimize geographic reach and delivery routes by establishing partnerships with nine businesses across the Inland Northwest Region to create new distribution locations, streamlining operations and broadening access to local food. The anticipated outcomes of this project include the creation of sustainable revenue streams for the food hub and its producers, ultimately leading to continuous consumer access to locally produced agricultural products. The beneficiaries of this project encompass a range of stakeholders, including farmers, ranchers, and agricultural processors, as well as consumers seeking access to fresh, regional food. Through these activities, LINC aims to revolutionize market access for its partners and facilitate the long-term coordination of the food chain, guaranteeing consistent supply and improved economic opportunities for all involved.

original_description: Simply Indiana was formed in early 2024, following close collaboration between MenuLogic K12, Wild Pansy Farm, and Indiana school food procurement specialists, facilitated by a 2023/24 Farm-to-School Action Planning Grant. The working group's research indicates Indiana's school nutrition programs (SNPs) cannot procure farm-raised foods at scale locally, due to such barriers as cost, seasonality, and the critical lack of infrastructure for aggregating and processing ingredients. The Simply Indiana Food Hub is acting upon this research in three areas of work: farm supply chain development, facilities construction, and product delivery to schools. This Local Food Promotion Program application formalizes the partnership between working group members, in order to concentrate funding on development of a software platform that connects SNPs with local producers. The Menu Logic K12 platform will help school districts publicize their demand for Indiana-origin ingredients and enable Simply Indiana to coordinate with local farms and schools to supply this demand. The beneficiaries include students, who will access healthier meals; local farmers and suppliers, who will gain new business opportunities; and SNPs, which will benefit from improved procurement processes and reduced administrative burdens. Through this collaborative effort, the project aims to foster sustainable demand for local ingredients.
updated_description: Simply Indiana was formed in early 2024, following close collaboration between MenuLogic K12, Wild Pansy Farm, and Indiana school food procurement specialists, facilitated by a 2023/24 Farm-to-School Action Planning Grant, to address significant challenges within Indiana’s school nutrition programs. The project’s purpose is to establish a software platform designed to connect school districts directly with local producers, enabling a more efficient and scalable procurement of farm-raised foods. This initiative will focus on three key areas: the development of farm supply chain networks, the construction of facilities to support aggregation and processing, and the coordinated delivery of products to schools. The anticipated outcomes include increased access to locally sourced ingredients for students, new business opportunities for farmers and processors, and streamlined procurement processes for school food programs, ultimately reducing administrative burdens. The primary beneficiaries of this collaborative effort include students who will benefit from improved nutritional quality in their meals, as well as farmers and processors who will gain access to a stable market for their goods. Furthermore, the school food programs themselves will experience enhanced efficiency and effectiveness in their operations. By fostering sustainable demand for local ingredients, Simply Indiana aims to strengthen the regional food system and support the economic viability of agricultural businesses throughout Indiana. This project represents a strategic investment in a more resilient and localized food supply chain.

original_description:
Navore Market's innovative online platform aims to invigorate local and regional food systems by connecting local producers directly and indirectly with businesses and consumers. The purpose is to optimize indirect marketing strategies with the online marketplace with features to increase cost-effective distribution methods, minimize on- farm waste, and strengthen relationships with help from parter and subaward recipient, li D Cuisine, the earth's tABLE. Activities include onboarding producers who conduct indirect sales, account set up, training sessions, enhancing distribution and wholesale features, connecting local producers with wholesale customers and local businesses, and creating individual plans to reduce on-farm waste.
Key deliverables are the continuous development of the Navore Market platform, recruitment of over 40 local producers that sell indirectly, at least 1 new or improved distribution plan per account, establishing new connections to local businesses and wholesale customers, 4 rounds of feature updates, 4 aggregation hubs established, and 10 producers who reduced on-farm waste. Resulting in  increased market access for producers, more efficient distribution networks, and a rise in the local food economy's vitality. Primary beneficiaries include small and medium-sized local food producers who will gain market exposure and business opportunities, as well as businesses and customers with increased access to local products.
updated_description: Navore Market’s innovative online platform aims to invigorate local and regional food systems by connecting local producers directly and indirectly with businesses and consumers. The project focuses on optimizing indirect marketing strategies through a new online marketplace, incorporating features designed to increase cost-effective distribution methods, minimize on-farm waste, and strengthen relationships with partner and subaward recipient, li D Cuisine, the earth’s tABLE. Key activities involve onboarding over 40 local producers who conduct indirect sales, establishing accounts, and creating individual plans to reduce on-farm waste. The project will also enhance distribution and wholesale features, connect these producers with wholesale customers and local businesses, and develop at least one new or improved distribution plan per account. Furthermore, four aggregation hubs will be established. Anticipated outcomes include increased market access for farmers, ranchers, and processors, more efficient distribution networks, and a rise in the local food economy’s vitality. The primary beneficiaries of this project are small and medium-sized local food producers who will gain enhanced market exposure and business opportunities, alongside businesses and consumers who will experience increased access to local products. The project will result in the continuous development of the Navore Market platform, the recruitment of the specified number of producers, the establishment of new connections to local businesses and wholesale customers, and the creation of four rounds of feature updates. Ultimately, this initiative seeks to foster a more robust and accessible local food system, supporting a range of stakeholders involved in the production and distribution of agricultural products.

original_description:
Fresh Food for Phoenix will utilize Sun Produce Cooperative's 35 years of experience and multiple connections to improve food systems and local food access, consumption of local food, and distribution in the Phoenix metropolitan area. Phoenix is the largest city in Arizona with a population of 1,608,190 (2020 Census) and the greater metropolitan area, including Mesa, Tempe, and Chandler, is nearly 5 million, meaning the potential to increase consumers of local food is tremendous. The proposed project will increase markets for 42 small farmers in the region, expand the Co-op's CSA program from the current 250 to 500 subscribers by year three, and promote Sun Produce Cooperative and local food through a marketing campaign while simultaneously reducing food waste on the farms included in the project. The Fresh Food for Phoenix CSA expansion will target low income/low access areas, focusing on reaching families at elementary schools.
Beneficiaries: Sales for small, local farmers will increase by 100% by year three as a result of doubling the CSA subscribers, benefiting 42 farmers. Of those, 36 are current Sun Produce Cooperative members, with 36% beginner farmers and 29% black, indigenous, or person of color (BIPOC). CSA locations to be added will target Title 1 (low-income) schools and/or areas of low food access. Of the current nine CSA sites, five are located in low income/low access areas. Of the 500 subscribers to be reached by year three, an estimated 250 will be residents of low income/low access areas.
updated_description: Fresh Food for Phoenix will establish a comprehensive initiative to bolster local food systems and expand access to fresh produce within the Phoenix metropolitan area, capitalizing on Sun Produce Cooperative’s 35 years of experience and extensive network of connections. The project anticipates increasing markets for 42 small farmers in the region, aiming to double the Cooperative’s CSA program from its current 250 subscribers to 500 by year three, alongside a targeted marketing campaign to promote Sun Produce Cooperative and locally sourced agricultural products. This expansion will specifically focus on reaching low-income/low access areas, with an estimated 250 of the 500 anticipated subscribers residing in these targeted locations, and will establish five new CSA locations within these areas, building upon the existing nine sites. The anticipated outcomes include a 100% increase in sales for the 42 participating farmers by year three, with 36 of these farmers being current members of Sun Produce Cooperative, representing a mix of experienced and beginner operations, and 29% of the farmers are BIPOC. The project will directly benefit ranchers, processors, and other stakeholders involved in the regional agricultural supply chain. By strategically increasing market opportunities for these farmers, Fresh Food for Phoenix intends to enhance the availability of locally grown food for consumers throughout the greater Phoenix area.

original_description: Veritable Vegetable is a unique company providing a range of grower and producer services including the collection, transportation, and wholesale distribution of farm products, and full-service freight and logistics. With our common carrier authority, we're remarkable among distribution companies in that we offer Less-than-Load (LTL) refrigerated freight services. The ability to transport relatively small quantities of food to different markets is critical to the survival of small and mid-sized regional producers. This project will enable local producers to develop new and diverse markets for their goods. Key activities: creating videos explaining different freight and logistic services available and how to use them effectively; conducting outreach to local/ regional producers; designing and launching a web-based transportation logistics platform; developing educational resources; and promoting the platform and resources widely. Expected outcomes and deliverables: a new freight booking platform, resources for freight and market readiness, a marketing and promotion plan,how-to' videos on how to use the new platform; and increased knowledge and use of our freight services. The primary beneficiaries are local/regional producers who will improve market readiness, increase engagement with market access points and local value chains, and increase their economic viability in a competitive marketplace. The project also benefits regional retailers, grocers, wholesalers, food hubs, distributors, and our own logistics operations.
updated_description: Veritable Vegetable is undertaking a project to enhance market access for local producers by creating a comprehensive freight booking platform and associated resources. The core activities include developing how-to videos explaining available freight and logistics services, conducting outreach to farmers and ranchers, designing and launching the new platform, and producing educational materials. Anticipated outcomes include a fully operational freight booking system, readily available resources for producers to assess their market readiness, and a marketing and promotion plan to drive adoption. The primary beneficiaries of this project are regional farmers, ranchers, processors, and other stakeholders involved in the supply chain, as well as local retailers, grocers, wholesalers, and food hubs who rely on access to fresh agricultural products. Veritable Vegetable aims to increase engagement with market access points and strengthen local value chains, ultimately improving the economic viability of these producers within a competitive marketplace. The project will deliver a streamlined system for booking freight services, providing producers with the tools needed to efficiently transport their goods to various destinations, while also benefiting regional food distribution networks. The expected result is a stronger, more connected food system, with Veritable Vegetable facilitating increased movement of agricultural products and expanding economic opportunities for its partners.

original_description:
ChopLocal's LFPP implementation project is focused on connecting, cultivating, and strengthening relationships between local and regional producers and local and regional food businesses and consumer-facing markets.
ChopLocal, an online farmer's market specifically for meat, seeks to increase and improve marketing efforts on behalf of participating producers by hiring a dedicated marketing specialist, revising and implementing the ChopLocal marketing plan, improving Search Engine Optimization and performing web development to maximize conversions, order size and order frequency. This project is expected to increase the online sales of participating producers by 25% year over year, and many of the activities included will have a lasting impact on sales volume after the grant period has ended.
updated_description: ChopLocal’s LFPP implementation project is focused on connecting, cultivating, and strengthening relationships between local and regional producers and local and regional food businesses and consumer-facing markets, aiming to significantly improve the marketing efforts for participating businesses. This project encompasses the hiring of a dedicated marketing specialist, a comprehensive revision and implementation of the ChopLocal marketing plan, and significant web development to maximize conversions, order size, and order frequency. Specifically, the project will focus on optimizing the online platform to drive increased sales volume among participating producers. The anticipated outcomes of this initiative include a year-over-year increase of 25% in the online sales generated by the involved farmers, ranchers, and food processors. These activities are designed to have a lasting positive impact on sales volume extending beyond the grant period. The primary beneficiaries of this project include the local farmers and ranchers who supply the product, as well as the consumer-facing businesses and the consumers themselves seeking access to locally sourced products. Ultimately, this project will strengthen the entire regional food system by facilitating greater market access for producers and improving the availability of locally produced goods for consumers.

original_description:
Strong local food systems are a crucial foundation for building resilient communities wherein farmers earn sustainable livings and all have access to healthy food. The continued disappearance of small farms nationally is a strong indication that innovative approaches are needed.
One such innovation is Argus Farm Stop which represents a breakthrough model to grow local food economies. Founded in 2014, Argus breaks the traditional local food system paradigm. Unlike in the industrial model, farms selling through Argus maintain their farm identities and pricing control and receive 70% of retail sales. Through this model, local farms and producers have been paid over $20 million over the past 10 years and the 2022 Ag Census reported the largest growth of new farms selling vegetables of any county in Michigan.
While progress has been made, distinct opportunities remain to expand the capacity and reach of our local food system. Here we propose to further extend the innovation of the farm stop model to
1) expand access to local food among low income, wholesale and institution customers, 2) expand off-season farm sales in January-May and 3) expand systems for aggregation, storage and distribution of local food. The resulting systems, approaches and impacts will be disseminated for the benefit of other food communities.
updated_description: Argus Farm Stop is undertaking a project to further expand the innovative farm stop model, a critical approach to building resilient local food economies. This project will focus on expanding access to locally produced agricultural products for wholesale and institutional customers, as well as establishing off-season sales during the January-May period, alongside the development of systems for aggregation, storage, and distribution of these goods. The anticipated outcome of this work is to significantly increase the volume of sales generated by local farms and producers, building upon the already substantial $20 million in payments received over the past decade. Specifically, the project aims to leverage the existing Argus model to support farmers and ranchers, processors, and other stakeholders within the local food system, contributing to the reported largest growth of new vegetable farms in Michigan as evidenced by the 2022 Ag Census. This expanded system will directly benefit farmers and consumers by providing increased market opportunities and access to fresh, locally grown food. The project will concentrate on streamlining the flow of products from production to distribution, improving the overall efficiency of the local food network. Ultimately, the project seeks to demonstrate and disseminate this model to other communities seeking to strengthen their local food economies, fostering a more robust and reliable supply of agricultural products.

original_description: Dakota Angus represents two, third generation livestock farms that have incorporated a value added farm to consumer beef program. The goal of this project is to build business capacity and expand customer base through both wholesale business and expanded direct to consumer distribution geography. We hope to add up to 5 new routes and expand wholesale business through grocery stores, food hubs, convenient stores, and schools in underserved markets. In ND, there are 34 counties that have low access to grocery stores, five times more than other rural areas nationally. Although agriculture is the top economic driver in North Dakota, livestock production only accounts for 8% of those economic dollars. It is critical to expand market opportunities that add value back to livestock producers. A study by the ND Public Health Association found that if each ND household spent just $10 a week on ND produced food, we could redirect $167 million each year to the state's food producers and recirculate that money in the local economy. Secondarily, we could create additional jobs and better protect our rural main streets and schools in the community where we live and work. We believe the beneficiaries of this project will be our community with at least two new jobs, additional livestock producers, and underserved communities.
updated_description: Dakota Angus seeks to build business capacity and expand its customer base through a strategic combination of wholesale distribution and expanded direct-to-consumer channels. This project will focus on establishing new distribution routes, targeting up to five additional locations, and increasing sales within grocery stores, food hubs, convenient stores, and schools, particularly in areas with limited access to fresh food options. The anticipated outcome of this initiative is a significant increase in the volume of Dakota Angus beef reaching consumers, directly supporting local ranchers and processors. The primary beneficiaries of this project include farmers and ranchers within the Dakota Angus operation, as well as consumers seeking locally produced beef. Furthermore, the project aims to strengthen rural communities by boosting economic activity and supporting local businesses. It is estimated that the project will generate at least two new jobs, providing additional economic opportunities within these communities. Dakota Angus’s strategy will contribute to a more robust local food system, with the goal of increasing the amount of locally produced beef available to consumers across North Dakota. The success of this endeavor will ultimately benefit a wide range of stakeholders involved in the production and distribution of high-quality beef.

original_description: The City of Tempe will implement a cooperative food business development program that provides underserved Tempe residents with access to free commercial kitchen space, bilingual business development training, and hyper­ local markets. This initiative will connect Tempe residents to the regional food system while developing opportunities for community wealth-building within the middle-of-the-supply-chain space. The project will transform a city-owned commercial kitchen space into a community kitchen through values-based programming that addresses residents' expressed interest in business development and incubation. The program will consist of four, 10-week-long sessions that equip participants with the necessary knowledge and skills to start and run worker-owned food processing businesses, focused on developing value-added goods. The program will engage residents from Northeast Tempe, an area that has been identified as a Low-income, Low-access community by the USDA. In addition to empowering 80 Tempe residents to develop worker-owned processing businesses, this project will embed the new cooperatives within the local food economy by developing new markets to purchase Arizona-grown produce and sell value-added goods in Tempe. By collaborating with public, private, and non-profit partners, this project will cultivate connections between Arizona growers, new food businesses, and neighborhood food outlets, allowing stakeholders from across the value chain to reap its benefits.
updated_description: The City of Tempe will implement a cooperative food business development program designed to connect Tempe residents with the regional food system and foster community wealth-building. This initiative will transform a city-owned commercial kitchen space into a community kitchen, equipping 80 Tempe residents with the resources to establish worker-owned food processing businesses focused on developing value-added goods. The program will facilitate the creation of new markets for Arizona-grown produce and the sale of these value-added goods within Tempe, engaging farmers, processors, and other stakeholders throughout the food value chain. The anticipated outcomes include the establishment of several new food businesses, increasing access to locally produced agricultural products for consumers and bolstering the economic viability of regional food operations. The project specifically targets residents from Northeast Tempe, a designated Low-income, Low-access community, offering them opportunities to participate directly in the supply chain. By building connections between growers and food outlets, the City of Tempe aims to strengthen the overall food system and create a more resilient local economy, supporting the development of regional food businesses and enhancing access to fresh, locally processed foods for the community.

original_description:
After more than a decade of progress from the Tyonek Grown program, the Native Village of Tyonek currently benefits from a strong local food system with greater access to locally produced foods than most remote villages in Alaska.
While socio-economic barriers persist, the proximity of Tyonek to Alaska's largest urban-center allows residents to benefit from access to the global food supply chain. Despite strong local and global food chains, and the robust food producing regions surrounding Tyonek, there remains no access to regionally produced foods due to its location off-the- road system. Thus, a regional food supply chain is a critical and missing element of ensuring a diverse and resilient food system in Tyonek. To address this gap, the Tyonek GATHER food hub will aggregate produce from small-scale and indigenous producers from surrounding communities, as well as support local food harvesters, producers, and traditional food processors in Tyonek through training and technical assistance.
In addition to food hub implementation, this project will accomplish a two-phase food system assessment to uncover the specific conditions and barriers impacting the food system in Tyonek and for Tyonek shareholders at large. To accomplish true food system resilience that ensures tribal food sovereignty in the face of crises, these assessments will shed light on existing gaps and barriers in Tyonek's food system, as well as create systems for gathering input on food system priorities.
updated_description: The Tyonek GATHER food hub project aims to establish a regional food supply chain for the Native Village of Tyonek, addressing a critical gap in access to locally produced foods. This project will facilitate the aggregation of produce from small-scale farmers and traditional food processors within surrounding communities, alongside supporting local food harvesters in Tyonek. The anticipated outcomes include the creation of a more resilient food system capable of supplying a broader range of agricultural products to the village’s residents. The project will support the establishment of a central location for collecting and distributing these goods, bolstering the overall food security of the Native Village of Tyonek and its shareholders. Ultimately, this initiative seeks to strengthen the food system for Tyonek’s consumers and stakeholders, providing a more reliable source of agricultural products. The project will focus on improving access to a variety of food sources for the village, benefiting farmers and processors alike.

original_description: Capital Roots’ Farm-to-Institution Program addresses the lack of connectivity between small-scale producers' desire to sell to institutions and the desire of institutions to purchase local food. Working with producers in the Capital Region’s food system, we will locate appropriately sized markets and increase access to quality food for institutional partners who serve underserved communities. This combination provides vital economic and social development to often overlooked communities and businesses. Through our Food Hub, institutions can purchase local farm products at competitive prices. This Program fills the fresh food gap, occupying a unique niche within our region by exclusively focusing on local food, providing higher quality, nutritional value and taste to community members and vital support to rural agricultural economies. With a new 4,000 square foot Food Hub, Capital Roots is poised to significantly expand its role as a producer-to-consumer intermediary in NY’s Capital Region. We enlisted five agricultural producers as collaborators- offering sales/marketing opportunities- and six institutions/schools who will purchase fresh food in underserved communities. With program expansion Capital Roots will support the operation of up to 50-plus producers in the 11-County Capital Region foodshed and 20 small-scale institutions and 10 schools. Capital Roots will partner with Brightside Up to connect with regional childcare centers to increase consumption of local food.
updated_description: Capital Roots’ Farm-to-Institution Program addresses the critical need for improved connections between small-scale producers and institutional food buyers within the Capital Region’s food system. This project focuses on establishing a new 4,000 square foot Food Hub, alongside partnerships with five agricultural producers and six institutions/schools, to facilitate the purchase of local farm products. The anticipated outcome is a significant expansion of access to high-quality food for consumers and stakeholders, particularly benefiting farmers and ranchers in the 11-County Capital Region foodshed. Specifically, the program aims to support the operation of up to 50-plus producers, providing a vital sales and marketing channel for their goods. The program will also enable the purchase of fresh food by these institutions, serving communities reliant on locally produced goods. Capital Roots’ efforts will contribute to strengthening the regional agricultural economy and increasing the availability of fresh food options for consumers. The organization will partner with Brightside Up to connect with regional childcare centers, further expanding the reach of this initiative. Ultimately, the Farm-to-Institution Program is designed to bolster the stability and growth of local agricultural businesses while simultaneously improving the food supply for the communities that depend on them.

original_description:
The proposed project, “Moving Invasive Species to Impactful Results: Creating Partnerships and Growing Markets for American Shad in the Pacific Northwest”, aims to enhance economic opportunities for tribal and non-tribal fishers and mid-tier operators working with an abundant, invasive, and nutritious fish species, American Shad (Alosa sapidissima), in the Columbia River region. Over the next three years, we aim to 1) Cultivate and connect mid-tier food enterprises, producers, and other through market development and value-chain coordination activities, 2) Incubate and grow mid-tier producers ability to develop value-added products and assess market opportunities for Shad through technical assistance services, and 3) Increase access and availability of American Shad products by coordinating regional distribution networks and establishing wholesale market and consumer connections. As a result of this work, we will establish a sustainable network of producers developing value-added products with American Shad and increase regional market demand for consumer tested products.
Native and non-native fishers will improve access to efficient processing, transportation and distribution channels supported by cooperative cost-sharing and resource allocation among producers and supply chain partners. Ecotrust will disseminate findings to support replication in and enhance economic benefit of those facing similar challenges of overabundance coupled with limited market opportunities.
updated_description: Moving Invasive Species to Impactful Results: Creating Partnerships and Growing Markets for American Shad in the Pacific Northwest aims to enhance economic opportunities for farmers, processors, and stakeholders working with an abundant, invasive, and nutritious fish species, American Shad (Alosa sapidissima), in the Columbia River region. Over the next three years, this project will focus on cultivating and connecting mid-tier food enterprises, producers, and other stakeholders through market development and value-chain coordination activities, as well as incubating and growing mid-tier producers’ ability to develop value-added products and assess market opportunities for Shad. Specifically, the project will increase access and availability of American Shad products by coordinating regional distribution networks and establishing wholesale market and consumer connections. The anticipated outcome is the establishment of a sustainable network of producers developing value-added products with American Shad and a corresponding increase in regional market demand for consumer tested products. This initiative will benefit farmers and processors by providing improved access to efficient processing, transportation, and distribution channels, supported by cooperative cost-sharing and resource allocation among producers and supply chain partners. The project’s success will be measured by the volume of American Shad products reaching the market, demonstrating a positive economic impact for the involved stakeholders.

awardee_name: The Research Foundation for SUNY on behalf of U. at Buffalo
original_description: Mobile markets are like farmers' markets on wheels that address food access disparities by selling affordable local produce in convenient locations across communities facing food apartheid. The growth of this innovative food access model has accelerated nationwide as mobile markets strengthen regional food systems through connecting growers with consumers and are able to meet the unique food needs of their target communities.
