The Veggie Van is an evidence based mobile market program that provides access to local and regionally produced food for the campus community at University at Buffalo (UB), the largest university in the State University of New York (SUNY) system, where more than half of the student body has reported experiencing food insecurity. This project will improve the reach and effectiveness of the UB Veggie Van by meeting the following objectives: 1) Increase local producer access to new markets, sales, and processing to create value added products in the form of ready-to-use products; 2) Increase food access through the adaption and implementation of the Veggie Van mobile market model to a campus setting; and 3) Raise awareness of locally produced food among the campus community through promotion of an Eat Local food campaign and pledge. Together these objectives will help expand access to locally grown and produced foods in underserved communities and connect producers with new markets.
updated_description: The Veggie Van project aims to expand access to locally produced food within the University at Buffalo (UB) campus community, addressing food access challenges faced by students. This project will focus on increasing local producer access to new markets, sales, and processing, specifically through the creation of ready-to-use products, and adapting and implementing the Veggie Van mobile market model within a campus setting. Anticipated outcomes include improved access to locally grown and produced foods for the campus community, bolstering regional food systems through connections between farmers and consumers. The primary beneficiaries of this project are the students and staff of UB, as well as the local producers who supply the market. The project seeks to strengthen relationships between stakeholders, promoting the availability of fresh food options. This initiative will support the development of new markets for agricultural products. The project will facilitate increased sales opportunities for farmers and ranchers. By establishing a mobile market on campus, the Veggie Van will support the efficient movement of goods from producers to consumers. The project's success will be measured by the volume of food distributed and the engagement of the campus community through the “Eat Local” food campaign and pledge.

original_description: The Chesapeake Farm to Institution Value Chain Coordination Project will demonstrate a replicable model for preparing both institutions and farmers to commit to larger local food sales transactions, leveraging important federal farm-to-school funding, and complying with state legislation on local foodl. It addresses the challenges institutions  have in transacting with small family farms, and prepares farmers to work within state institutions and public school procurement processes. This project will: (1) delvelop strategies to expand local food in institutions, (2) identify and support farmers interested to work in those markets, (3) help create individual institutional demand plans, and coordinate farmers' sales to meet those plans, identifying the best logistics for them, leading to purchasing commitments, and (4) document and make permanent the value chain coordination processes with farmers, instituional  buyers, and partnewers in the supply chain: Departments of Agriculture, Food Counciles, regional hospitals, and distributors. Institutional budyers, farmers, distributors, partnewrs will callaborate, 20 institutions will commit to purchases from local farmers, endabling potentially 120,00 university students, 200,00 K-12 students, 4,000 patients, and institutional employess to access local nutritious food. Four distributors and food hubs in these states will incorporate local farmers into their supply chain, and 20 farmers will report increased whole sale revenues.
updated_description: The Chesapeake Farm to Institution Value Chain Coordination Project aims to establish a replicable model for facilitating transactions between institutions and local farmers, leveraging federal farm-to-school funding and state legislation. This project will focus on addressing the challenges institutions face when working with smaller farms and preparing farmers to operate within state institutional and public school procurement processes. Specifically, the project will develop strategies to expand local food purchases within institutions, identify and support farmers interested in supplying those markets, and coordinate farmers’ sales to meet established institutional demand plans, while simultaneously optimizing logistics and securing purchasing commitments. Furthermore, the project will meticulously document and permanently establish value chain coordination processes involving farmers, institutional buyers, and key supply chain partners, including Departments of Agriculture, Food Councils, regional hospitals, and distributors. A key component involves incorporating four distributors and food hubs into the supply chain, with the anticipated outcome being that 20 farmers will report increased wholesale revenues. Ultimately, this coordinated effort seeks to enable approximately 120,000 university students, 200,000 K-12 students, 4,000 patients, and institutional employees to access locally sourced, nutritious food. The project anticipates a positive impact on farmers and other stakeholders involved in the food supply chain, and aims to improve access to local food products for a significant population of consumers.

original_description: This Project will expand on recommendations in the Colorado Farm to Loading Dock Assessment Report and build on Nourish Colorado’s RFSP grant, a project that has collected procurement data (what products are purchased, how often) from participating institutional meal programs. This data will be collated in late 2024 to develop a shared, cross-institutional RFP to support a collaborative bidding process for regional suppliers in early 2025. The goal of this Project is to strengthen the collaboration of small- and mid-sized producers, food hubs, and incubators in southeast Colorado to catalyze sustainable, regional procurement, aggregation, processing, and distribution by leveraging local food in institutions. The data collected through the RFSP Project will be used to identify commonly purchased products, with the intention of identifying at least four products that could be supplied locally—a critical step to increase participation of local suppliers and their engagement in a long-term bid process, and ultimately sustainable regional value chains. Nourish Colorado will also provide TA to support partners with the aggregation, processing, and distribution of these four products to institutional buyers. The Project will allow key players to learn more about value chain logistics; receive food safety education; bolster the regional bid with additional items; help inform institutional regional bids; and further an aggregation hub that connects food hubs to local producers.
updated_description: Nourish Colorado’s project aims to strengthen regional food systems in southeast Colorado by expanding upon data collected through a recent procurement assessment. This initiative will develop a collaborative, cross-institutional Request for Proposals (RFP) process, targeted at regional suppliers, to facilitate the purchase of commonly used food products. The core of the project involves identifying at least four products that can be supplied locally by regional farmers, food hubs, and processing facilities, with the goal of creating sustainable value chains. Successful completion of this project will benefit a range of stakeholders, including farmers, ranchers, and food processors, by increasing access to institutional purchasing opportunities. The anticipated outcomes include the establishment of streamlined aggregation, processing, and distribution networks, ultimately supporting the efficient movement of regional food products to institutional buyers. Nourish Colorado will provide support to these stakeholders regarding logistical aspects and food safety procedures. This will bolster regional bidding processes with additional items, and further an aggregation hub that connects food hubs to local producers, thereby increasing the volume of locally sourced food utilized by institutions. The project intends to provide the necessary support to facilitate the procurement of these goods, contributing to a more robust and resilient food system throughout the region.

original_description: Cart Organics (FCO), a food hub comprised of small farms in Ventura and Santa Barbara counties along the Southern California coast; will implement a strategic plan to gain new institutional partners, and increase school districts served in their current Ventura County School Food Hub Project (VCF2S). Since Fall 2023, this project has achieved over $400K in sales to 62 schools across 5 districts, serving 52,000 students. This project will assist the food hub to obtain group-based GAP certification, develop and market value-added products, and increase deliveries. Exploring partnerships with universities, Food-As-Medicine programs, and corrections facilities will inform development of processed products and crop offerings   – mix of products both fresh and processed – offered for sale.  New institutional partners will increase the quantity and variety of crops sold, while creating stability when schools are closed.
updated_description: Cart Organics, a food hub operating in Ventura and Santa Barbara counties, is undertaking a strategic plan to expand its reach and impact within the school food system. The project’s primary purpose is to secure new institutional partnerships and increase the number of school districts served as part of the Ventura County School Food Hub Project (VCF2S). Since Fall 2023, this initiative has successfully generated over $400,000 in sales to 62 schools across five districts, supplying food to approximately 52,000 students. This expansion will be achieved through the acquisition of group-based Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) certification, the development and marketing of value-added products, and an increase in delivery operations. The project anticipates a broadened selection of products, encompassing both fresh and processed goods, catering to the varied needs of the schools. The anticipated outcome is the increased availability of locally produced agricultural products to a wider range of consumers and stakeholders, creating stability for the food hub when school closures occur. Ultimately, the beneficiaries of this project include the farmers and ranchers who supply the food hub, the schools seeking to provide nutritious meals to their students, and the processors involved in transforming the agricultural products into marketable goods. This project will strengthen the local food supply chain and ensure a reliable source of fresh and processed food for the students and communities it serves.

original_description:
The Marion Barry Avenue Market project’s goal is to launch a multi-purpose food hub in the heart of a community that lacks equitable access to healthy food and economic opportunity. Dreaming Out Loud is a nonprofit farm, food hub, and entrepreneurial incubator. Our mission is to create economic opportunities for the DC metro region’s marginalized communities by building a healthy, equitable food system. Last year, we acquired a large retail space in DC’s historic Anacostia neighborhood. This 4,770-square-foot, formerly abandoned building, is a vibrant and innovative space that tackles the complex issue of food insecurity in our nation’s capital. It includes a food hub, a grocery store, a food incubator for farmers and entrepreneurs, and a community cafe. The Marion Barry Avenue Market building is a new and larger home for several of Dreaming Out Loud’s already successful food distribution programs. In May 2024, we will open this much needed community resource. With support from the USDA, we will be able to implement and expand programming in the space over the next two years. This project will 
benefit people in the surrounding community, many of whom experience extreme food insecurity because they have limited access to quality grocery stores and fresh produce. In addition to being a place to access high-quality, fresh, healthy, affordable produce for folks from Ward 7 and 8, it will also allow Dreaming Out Loud to hire folks from the Anacostia community. Finally, it will support historically underserved farmers in our region.
updated_description: Dreaming Out Loud is launching the Marion Barry Avenue Market, a multi-purpose food hub in the heart of the Anacostia neighborhood of Washington, D.C., designed to address food insecurity and create economic opportunities. This new facility encompasses a food hub, a grocery store, a food incubator for farmers and ranchers, and a community cafe, occupying a 4,770-square-foot space that was previously vacant. The anticipated outcome of this project is to provide access to high-quality, fresh produce for consumers in Ward 7 and 8, while simultaneously supporting local food businesses and increasing the availability of regionally produced agricultural products. The primary beneficiaries of the Marion Barry Avenue Market include residents of the surrounding communities, as well as stakeholders throughout the food system. This market will serve as a vital resource, offering access to nutritious food options and supporting the operational needs of food producers and processors. The project’s success will be measured by the increased flow of locally sourced agricultural products through the hub and the sustained viability of the grocery store and food incubator. By establishing a central location for food distribution, Dreaming Out Loud intends to strengthen the local food network and contribute to a more secure and resilient food supply for the community.

original_description:
The Food Conservancy, Inc., (501c3) and its working arm, Good Nature Family Farms (GNFF), proposes to strengthen the gaps in the local food-supply chain in Missouri. The gaps often stem from post- harvest barriers that have historically prohibited small to mid-sized farms from successfully entering a viable market and ultimately has resulted in many farms closing down. This has led to local food sources drying up and an increase in food-insecurity in our under-served communities.

GNFF's proposal is to enhance the sustainability of Missouri's local farms by establishing a new food system infrastructure and taking advantage of economies of scale. GNFF will utilize space in an existing grocery’s warehouse in a promise-zone in the North-side community of St. Louis, Missouri. The goal is to establish and expand the aggregation, processing, and distribution capacity of locally-grown and produced foods. GNFF will focus on local and regional producers, with emphasis on new, minority and women-owned growers.

As it has done for 100 Kansas City producers beginning in 1995, GNFF will create new connections to local, independent grocers. The major outcomes are 1) A replicable model of systemic change toward a more equitable outcome for 50 local producers, thereby escalating their economic sustainability and 2) Increased local food availability; thereby contributing to improved public health.
updated_description: The Food Conservancy, Inc., (501c3) and its working arm, Good Nature Family Farms (GNFF), proposes a project to strengthen the local food-supply chain in Missouri, addressing barriers that have historically prevented small to mid-sized farms from successfully entering viable markets and leading to farm closures. This initiative centers on establishing a new food system infrastructure by utilizing space within an existing grocery’s warehouse in a promise-zone located in the North-side community of St. Louis, Missouri. The project focuses on the aggregation, processing, and distribution of locally-grown and produced foods, with a key emphasis on connecting with local and regional producers. GNFF will actively seek to expand its relationships with farmers and ranchers, while simultaneously increasing the capacity to serve consumers through a network of independent grocers. The anticipated outcome of this project is a replicable model of systemic change, aiming to support 50 local producers and enhance their economic sustainability. Ultimately, this project intends to increase local food availability, which will contribute to improved public health outcomes for the community. The primary beneficiaries of this project include farmers, ranchers, processors, and other stakeholders within the Missouri agricultural sector.

original_description:
Prairieland Market seeks to open a new facility that will increase capacity with an on-site commercial kitchen, increased storage capacity for local food from area farmers, better access to healthy foods for those facing food insecurity, and an expansion of healthy food offerings to the community at large.
A key piece of this project is the establishment of a commercial kitchen on-site that will enable Prairieland Market to process more value-added products using local produce, meat, honey, cheese, and eggs.
Crucial to this expansion is the ability for area farmers to store more product for consumer sales, the CSA program, and value-added food production. Farmers that we currently buy from have stated that they could provide more product if we had the space. Additionally, having a long list of producers who would like to connect to consumers through Prairieland Market, but simply not having the capacity to add them.
An important component of this project is the marketing and promotion of local foods. By partnering with our producers, we will highlight the local food products that are available from each of those partners through a coordinated integrated marketing program.

By relocating and investing in a larger footprint, new equipment (including an on-site commercial kitchen), backroom and storage, the proposed project addresses the identified needs: to expand capacity and access; increase value-added food production; and grow the awareness and purchase of local food.
updated_description: Prairieland Market seeks to establish a new facility designed to significantly expand its capacity and improve access to local food products within the community. This project will involve the construction of a commercial kitchen on-site, enabling the processing of value-added products from local ingredients such as produce, meat, honey, cheese, and eggs, alongside increased storage capacity for farmers’ goods. Crucially, the facility will accommodate a greater volume of products for sale through the Customer Supported Agriculture (CSA) program and for use in value-added food production by processors and ranchers. Currently, numerous producers have expressed a desire to supply Prairieland Market, but limited space has prevented their inclusion. The project anticipates a substantial increase in the availability of locally produced goods to consumers and farmers alike, ultimately supporting a coordinated integrated marketing program to highlight these offerings. By expanding its operations, Prairieland Market intends to strengthen its role as a central hub for local food distribution, benefiting farmers, ranchers, and consumers seeking access to fresh, regional products. The anticipated outcomes include a broadened selection of food items, increased volume of local sales, and enhanced awareness of the value of regional food systems. The primary beneficiaries of this project are the farmers and ranchers who will have increased opportunities for sales and the consumers who will gain access to a greater variety of locally produced food.

original_description:
The purpose of this project is to increase access to markets for local BIPOC growers and at the same time expand access to fresh, local produce among low-income populations.
To achieve the project purpose, The Food Group will establish our Fare For All affordable grocery program as a consistent market for farmers of color (objective 1). To that end, we will develop transportation solutions for local growers who experience barriers delivering their produce to The Food Group's warehouse in New Hope. In addition, we will increase capacity for produce storage at The Food Group's warehouse. As a second objective, The Food Group will establish and strengthen purchasing relationships with BIPOC growers. To promote equitable purchasing relationships, The Food Group will adopt a tiered purchasing system and create simple contract processes for farmers. Finally, The Food Group will build interest in local products among Fare For All customers through marketing and promotional efforts (objective 3).

This project will benefit BIPOC growers in Minnesota, and in particular farmers at Big River Farms. In addition, the project will benefit low-income customers of The Food Group's Fare For All program.

Our key partner is Naima's Farm, a first-generation family farm that will serve as a docking station for the project collaborators. Collaborators include farm hubs Kilimo Minnesota, Sudanese Farming Group, and Route 1.
updated_description: The Food Group’s project aims to increase access to markets for local farmers and expand access to fresh produce among consumers. This initiative will establish a consistent market through the Food Group’s Fare For All affordable grocery program, focusing on purchasing produce from farmers of color. To facilitate this, The Food Group will develop transportation solutions for growers, particularly those facing delivery barriers to the New Hope warehouse, and will increase capacity for produce storage at the facility. Furthermore, The Food Group will establish and strengthen purchasing relationships with BIPOC growers utilizing a tiered purchasing system and simplified contract processes. Anticipated outcomes include increased sales for farmers and a greater availability of fresh, local products for Fare For All customers. The primary beneficiaries of this project are local farmers, especially those at Big River Farms, and the consumers participating in The Food Group’s Fare For All program. The project’s success relies on collaborative partnerships, notably with Naima’s Farm as a key docking station, along with farm hubs Kilimo Minnesota, Sudanese Farming Group, and Route 1. By streamlining the flow of produce from farms to consumers, The Food Group intends to support local agricultural businesses and ensure a reliable supply of fresh produce to the community.

original_description:
The project's purpose it to increase economic opportunity for small-scale, racially diverse produce farmers in Minnesota by facilitating access to new markets, particularly retail grocery. This project will provide farmers with technical assistance to achieve certifications like Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) and create food safety plans. The Good Acre’s Market Access team and 1201 Partners will educate new wholesale buyers on working with local distributors and expand sales through marketing, promotion, and building relationships. Specific effort will be made in partnership with Lunds & Byerlys to enter grocery retail. We will improve local food supply chain logistics through cross-docking, backhauling, and operation efficiencies. We will expand opportunities for small-scale farmers from $1.7 million to $3 million in annual purchases. This project will improve local food supply chain resilience and generate cost and time savings for farmers and partners. Technical assistance will increase the number of GAP certified farmers in Minnesota.

Beneficiaries: BIPOC produce farmers in Minnesota, particularly those growing on 10 acres or less; consumers seeking local and equitably sourced produce; and local food system partners including buyers and agricultural organizations.
updated_description: Good Acre’s Market Access project aims to increase economic opportunity for small-scale produce farmers in Minnesota by facilitating access to new markets, particularly retail grocery operations. The project will support farmers in achieving certifications like Good Agricultural Practices and creating food safety plans, alongside efforts to educate wholesale buyers on working with local distributors and expand sales through marketing and relationship building. A key focus is partnership with Lunds & Byerlys to establish a presence in grocery retail, while simultaneously improving local food supply chain logistics through cross-docking, backhauling, and operational efficiencies. This initiative anticipates expanding opportunities for small-scale farmers, increasing annual purchases from $1.7 million to $3 million. The project will bolster local food system resilience and generate cost and time savings for farmers and their partners. By supporting farmers in attaining GAP certification, the project expects to significantly increase the number of certified producers across the state. The primary beneficiaries of this project include farmers cultivating produce on 10 acres or less, consumers seeking locally sourced produce, and a range of food system partners such as buyers and agricultural organizations. Furthermore, this project seeks to strengthen the overall Minnesota food supply chain.

original_description:
Building on the findings of our 2022 LFPP planning grant, the Land Stewardship Project (LSP) and partners will 1) Increase wholesale readiness and food safety practices of local producers; 2) Increase farmer income through sales to local wholesale buyers including schools and food access programs; 3) Increase market access for producers by educating wholesale buyers and connecting them with local producers; 4) Increase local food access through local foods sales to schools, food access programs, and food businesses, and 5) Expand and strengthen private-public partnerships focused on the expansion of the local food economy in west central Minnesota.

Beneficiaries of this project include 45 farmers will increase revenue through sales to regional markets, more than 1900 consumers who will experience increased access to local foods via schools and local direct- to-consumer outlets, and 14 food service workers who will receive training on sourcing local foods.
LSP will engage a range of partners in this project, many of whom are members of the Minnesota Valley Local Foods Network (MVLFN), a working group established as a result of LSP's 2022 planning grant. Project partners include farmers, regional food hubs and distributors, local businesses, institutions (including schools and food access programs), economic development agencies, and nonprofit organizations.
updated_description: The Land Stewardship Project (LSP) will undertake a project focused on expanding the local food economy in west central Minnesota, aiming to increase wholesale readiness and food safety practices among local producers, thereby boosting farmer income through sales to regional markets and expanding market access for producers by educating wholesale buyers and connecting them with local suppliers. This project anticipates several key outcomes, including enhanced access to local foods for consumers via schools and direct-to-consumer outlets, and increased sales for farmers and ranchers. Specifically, the project will support 45 farmers, contributing to greater revenue streams, and will provide increased access to local foods for approximately 1,900 consumers. Furthermore, the project will support 14 food service workers in sourcing local food products. The Land Stewardship Project will collaborate with a range of partners, including members of the Minnesota Valley Local Foods Network, to achieve these goals. These stakeholders encompass farmers, regional food hubs and distributors, local businesses, institutions (such as schools and food access programs), and economic development agencies. The project’s anticipated benefits include facilitating the operation of shared-use kitchens and food hubs, contributing to a more robust and resilient local food system.

original_description:
The project seeks to primarily address small farm business sustainability, and fresh produce access in rural, low income or low access areas in the Mississippi Delta. The project proposes activities to facilitate capacity building and market integration support for 30+ small locally owned and operated farm businesses by providing training, technical assistance, and support needed to access new markets. The project will also develop new market channels for local producers including a mobile produce market which will connect farmers with programs such as the Local Food Purchase Assistance Program.

The project's objectives are:
1.	Increase market integration opportunities for small local growers
2.	Strengthen existing and develop new market channels supported by small local growers
3.	Increase fresh food access in rural Delta communities

The expected outcomes include:
1.	Increase access to processing and transportation capacity to access new markets
2.	Increase access to training and technical assistance
3.	Increase in the number of targeted farmers with wholesale and retail supplier agreements/contracts
4.	Increase the number of direct buyers to access fresh locally grown produce
5.	Increase of produce sales
6.	Reduction in on farm food waste
7.	Increase in economic sustainability among small women and minority owned farm businesses
updated_description: The project seeks to address small farm business sustainability and fresh produce access in rural, low-income or low-access areas of the Mississippi Delta. This initiative proposes activities to facilitate capacity building and market integration support for over 30 small, locally owned and operated farm businesses, providing them with the necessary training, technical assistance, and support to access new markets. A key component of this effort involves the development of new market channels, including a mobile produce market designed to connect farmers with programs such as the Local Food Purchase Assistance Program. Anticipated outcomes include increased access to processing and transportation capacity, allowing farmers to efficiently reach new markets and expand their sales. Furthermore, the project aims to bolster the number of targeted farmers with wholesale and retail supplier agreements/contracts, facilitating consistent market access. The project also expects to see an increase in the number of direct buyers accessing fresh, locally grown produce and a corresponding rise in overall produce sales. To minimize waste, the project anticipates a reduction in on-farm food waste. Ultimately, the project intends to foster economic sustainability among small farm businesses, with a particular focus on supporting small businesses owned by individuals. The project will directly benefit farmers, ranchers, and processors within the Delta region, alongside consumers seeking access to fresh, local food sources. The project’s success will be measured by the growth of these businesses and the increased availability of locally produced goods within the target communities.

original_description: This project Grow Together RI will enhance Rhode Island's mid-tier value chain and regional food system as Hope & Main expands to Providence. By providing production support, business assistance, and sales opportunities to producers/processors engaged in value-added production-- 62% of whom now use local agricultural products-- this project elevates items made with local agricultural commodities such as CPG items, baked goods, and prepared food.
updated_description: Grow Together RI is designed to enhance Rhode Island’s mid-tier value chain and regional food system as Hope & Main expands to Providence. This project focuses on elevating items produced using local agricultural commodities, including CPG items, baked goods, and prepared foods, with 62% of participating producers/processors now utilizing local agricultural products. The project’s primary goal is to increase the availability of these value-added products within the regional market. Anticipated outcomes include a strengthened local food system and increased market access for farmers and processors. The project will directly benefit stakeholders involved in the production and distribution of these goods, along with the consumers who purchase them. By supporting producers and processors, the project intends to build a more robust and resilient regional food network. The project’s success will be measured by the volume of locally produced goods reaching the market and the overall growth of the value chain. Ultimately, Grow Together RI seeks to create a greater connection between producers and consumers, fostering a thriving regional food system that supports local agriculture.

original_description: This project is Located in Norwich, Vermont, Willing Hands recovers surplus healthy food from grocery stores, wholesalers and farms and delivers it for free to more than 85 social service organizations across the Upper Valley region of Vermont and New Hampshire. Willing Hands’ mission is to reduce food waste and expand equitable and reliable access to fresh food.
updated_description: Willing Hands operates in Norwich, Vermont, with the purpose of recovering surplus, healthy food from grocery stores, wholesalers, and farms across the Upper Valley region of Vermont and New Hampshire. The organization then delivers this food free of charge to more than 85 social service organizations, significantly reducing food waste and expanding reliable access to fresh food for a range of stakeholders, including farmers, ranchers, and processors. This initiative anticipates a measurable impact through the consistent redistribution of edible food, supporting the operational needs of social service agencies and ultimately benefiting the communities they serve. The anticipated outcomes include a decrease in the amount of food discarded and an increase in the availability of fresh food options for individuals relying on these organizations. Specifically, Willing Hands’ work will aid those organizations in providing nourishment to their clients, ensuring access to nutritious food sources. The beneficiaries of this project are the various social service organizations and the individuals they support within the Upper Valley region. By efficiently collecting and distributing surplus food, Willing Hands directly contributes to improving food security and reducing waste within the local food system, while supporting the operations of vital community support networks.

original_description: Roots & Fruits is an online market and delivery solution that supports local and regional agricultural producers in Southern California, specifically Socially Disadvantaged Farmers and Ranchers. Producers with limited technical capabilities and time can sell merchandise through an online market without the need to manage or create their own website or manage logistics and delivery. Roots & Fruits handles the entire process for them from Farm to Table, so producers can focus more on farming. Roots & Fruits will increase capacity for 113 producers (Ag and value-added) in San Bernardino County, as well as increase access to local foods for the underserved tri-city desert communities of Barstow, Victorville, and Hesperia, CA. Through collaboration with subawardee, the Barstow Youth Sports Coalition– organizer of the only farmers market in Barstow– we aim to bridge the gap that exists between producers and consumers in the desert. Our collaborators will engage with beneficiaries by conducting producer/consumer surveys, listening sessions, and other methods of engagement to obtain feedback that will be critical for improving user experience. By leveraging our online market platform, optimized logistics/delivery, and data-driven decision-making, projects like Roots & Fruits not only modernize local food systems, but also serve as blueprints for adapting and enhancing agricultural practices across the nation. Expected outcomes include increased technological capacity of local/region.
updated_description: Roots & Fruits is an online market and delivery solution designed to support local and regional agricultural producers in Southern California, specifically Socially Disadvantaged Farmers and Ranchers, by providing a streamlined platform to sell their products directly to consumers. This project will facilitate the establishment of an online marketplace, optimizing logistics and delivery operations, enabling 113 producers – encompassing both agricultural and value-added processors – within San Bernardino County to expand their market reach. The project aims to bridge the gap between these producers and consumers in the tri-city desert communities of Barstow, Victorville, and Hesperia, collaborating with the Barstow Youth Sports Coalition to conduct producer/consumer surveys and engagement sessions, gathering critical feedback to continually improve the user experience. Anticipated outcomes include a significant increase in the capacity of local agricultural stakeholders to access markets and enhance the availability of regionally produced goods. The project will benefit farmers, ranchers, processors, and consumers alike, offering a modern approach to local food systems. Ultimately, Roots & Fruits seeks to strengthen the overall agricultural landscape, providing a robust and accessible channel for producers to connect with their customer base.

original_description: The Puget Sound Food Hub (PSFH) proposes partnering with the Northwest Agriculture Business Center (NABC) to solicit regional food systems stakeholders' input and create a business plan and capital plan supporting the expansion of its farmer-owned cooperative food hub. Collaborators include five regional Food Hubs, WSU Pierce County Extension, a cooperative grocer, and two organizations serving historically underrepresented communities. Information from these sessions will inform the development of a business plan and capital plan supporting a central distribution facility that increases sales opportunities for over 300 existing cooperative members, provides access to new markets for a conservatively estimated forty small farms that are not currently cooperative members, serves over 1600 existing co-op grocery customers and over 3400 existing food hub customer, and creates efficiencies that will reduce the Hubs' collective carbon food print. Completed plans will be presented at a stakeholder summit to garner feedback. Project outcomes will include an educated, engaged, and diverse community food systems stakeholders, who contribute to the development of a tenable business plan; the completion of a business plan supporting expansion of a mid-tier value chain network that creates opportunity and equity for regional producers; and the completion of a capital plan that details how the expansion will be funded.
updated_description: The Puget Sound Food Hub proposes to partner with the Northwest Agriculture Business Center to develop a comprehensive business and capital plan supporting the expansion of its farmer-owned cooperative food hub. This project will involve gathering input from a broad range of regional food systems stakeholders, including five regional food hubs, WSU Pierce County Extension, a cooperative grocer, and two organizations serving communities, to create a detailed plan. The anticipated outcomes of this initiative are an educated and engaged group of farmers, ranchers, processors, and stakeholders who will contribute to the development of a viable business plan. Specifically, the project will support the creation of a central distribution facility designed to increase sales opportunities for over 300 existing cooperative members and provide access to new markets for approximately forty small farms currently not part of the cooperative. Furthermore, the expanded food hub will serve over 1,600 existing co-op grocery customers and over 3,400 existing food hub customers, while simultaneously creating efficiencies that will reduce the collective carbon footprint of the hubs. The completion of these plans will be presented at a stakeholder summit to obtain valuable feedback. Ultimately, this project aims to foster a tenable business plan that creates opportunities and equity for regional producers, along with a detailed capital plan outlining how the expansion will be funded.

original_description: The AgriCluster Resilience and Expansion (ACRE) model will address systemic issues faced by Puerto Rico's agriculture sector. The project will transform informal collaborations among local farmers, agritourism operators, and stakeholders into resilient and competitive AgriClusters. Currently, these informal collaborations lack strategic structure, limiting the competitiveness, innovation, and market access of agricultural businesses in the Utuado municipality.
updated_description: The AgriCluster Resilience and Expansion (ACRE) model seeks to address systemic challenges confronting Puerto Rico’s agricultural sector, specifically within the Utuado municipality. This project will transform existing informal collaborations among local farmers, agritourism operators, and other stakeholders into resilient and competitive AgriClusters. The core of this initiative involves fostering strategic structures to enhance the competitiveness, innovation, and market access for agricultural businesses. The anticipated outcomes of this project include the development of strengthened regional food systems and increased access to agricultural products for consumers. Ultimately, the project will benefit farmers and ranchers by creating opportunities to expand their operations and reach new markets. Furthermore, the project aims to elevate the capacity of food processors and related businesses within the region. By establishing these AgriClusters, the project intends to streamline the flow of goods from producers to consumers, contributing to a more robust and efficient local food system. The project will provide a framework for greater collaboration and coordination among all involved parties, leading to improved market opportunities and economic viability for agricultural enterprises. The ultimate goal is to bolster the overall strength and sustainability of the agricultural sector in Utuado, supporting local livelihoods and strengthening the regional economy.

awardee_name: The Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma Health Sc
original_description:
The Oklahoma Local Agriculture Collaborative's (OLAC) mission is to unite partner agencies with agriculture entrepreneurs to ensure that the needs of local agribusinesses are recognized and represented. OLAC serves as an outlet to test and explore innovative ideas and provide technical guidance to grow the local food system. OLAC will work to assess the current market for local food in central Oklahoma through surveys and interviews with producers and indirect food procurement institutions (i.e. restaurants, distributors). Through the assessment, OLAC will identify barriers and facilitators in local food procurement. OLAC will then work with stakeholders to develop resources and trainings to be utilized by producers and markets, fostering sustainable outlets and mutually-beneficial purchasing practices for each entity.
A needs assessment in 2021 found that 54% of direct-to-consumer agriculture entrepreneurs (n=l 13) produced more than they could sell, or had the capacity to sell more, a follow-up assessment in 2023 showed that this increased to 84% (n=132). Oklahoma agriculture entrepreneurs have the capacity to expand and with strategic planning the indirect market will benefit. This project will cultivate Oklahoma's food procurement network through the development of training materials designed specifically to overcome these barriers in purchasing local agricultural products that meet the needs of both agriculture entrepreneurs and food procuring businesses.
updated_description: The Oklahoma Local Agriculture Collaborative’s (OLAC) project aims to strengthen Oklahoma’s food procurement network by developing targeted resources to address the challenges faced by local agricultural businesses. Specifically, OLAC will conduct a comprehensive assessment of the current market for local food within central Oklahoma, surveying farmers, ranchers, processors, and indirect food procurement institutions to identify barriers and facilitators in purchasing agricultural products. This assessment will ultimately lead to the creation of resources designed to support increased sales capacity for these producers and to facilitate mutually-beneficial purchasing practices between agricultural businesses and food procuring institutions. The anticipated outcome of this project is to increase the volume of local agricultural products available within the central Oklahoma market. The primary beneficiaries of this project include Oklahoma farmers, ranchers, and processors who currently experience challenges in selling their products to full capacity, as well as the institutions that purchase these products. By streamlining the purchasing process and providing tailored support, OLAC seeks to build a more robust and efficient food procurement network within the state. This collaborative effort promises to improve access to local food sources for consumers and strengthen the overall agricultural economy of Oklahoma.

awardee_name: Georgia Fruit & Vegetables Growers Association, Inc.
original_description: This pivotal feasibility study will evaluate the best path to success for an innovative mobile processing concept that not only adds value and extends shelf life but also minimizes waste in Georgia's fresh harvest in a region where 90% of Georgia’s 1200 produce farmers operate. Led by seasoned farmers, industry organizations, and subject matter experts and with comprehensive farmer feedback guiding the study, we will tackle one of the most pressing challenges in global food supply.
updated_description: This pivotal feasibility study will evaluate the best path to success for an innovative mobile processing concept focused on adding value and extending the shelf life of Georgia’s fresh harvest, addressing a critical challenge within the state’s agricultural sector. The project aims to minimize waste associated with produce handling and transportation, particularly within a region where 90% of Georgia’s 1200 produce farmers operate, representing a significant opportunity to improve efficiency and reduce losses. This study will thoroughly assess methods for processing agricultural goods, culminating in a strategic plan to optimize the flow of fresh products from farm to market. The anticipated outcomes of this initiative include a robust framework for mobile processing operations, streamlining the handling and preservation of Georgia’s abundant harvests. The primary beneficiaries of this project will be the farmers who supply the state’s produce, along with the processors involved in transforming agricultural commodities into marketable goods. Furthermore, this project will benefit the consumers who ultimately access these fresh products, and all stakeholders involved in the agricultural supply chain. The study will ultimately support the creation of a system that provides greater access to high-quality produce, bolstering the economic viability of the farming community and enhancing the availability of fresh food for market consumption.

original_description: This project is intended to perform in depth interviews and industry research to assess the supply, support, and market conditions that are currently affecting the survivability and success of cheese producers from Vermont. Cheese provides over $650million in annual revenue and represents the largest portion of agricultural revenue for Vermont, where it is also a critical cornerstone for tourism.
updated_description: Vermont’s cheese industry, representing over $650 million in annual revenue and the largest portion of agricultural revenue for the state, is the focus of this project, which seeks to conduct in-depth interviews and industry research to thoroughly assess the supply, support, and market conditions currently affecting the survivability and success of Vermont’s cheese producers. This research will concentrate on gathering detailed information regarding the challenges and opportunities facing farmers, processors, and other stakeholders within the Vermont cheese sector. The anticipated outcome of this project is to develop a comprehensive understanding of the factors influencing the industry’s performance, ultimately informing strategies to bolster the continued growth and stability of this vital component of Vermont’s economy. The primary beneficiaries of this project include Vermont’s cheese producers and the consumers who value locally produced goods. The research will directly impact the businesses involved in the production and distribution of cheese, strengthening their position within the market. Furthermore, the insights gained will be valuable to those involved in the sale and distribution of Vermont cheese, contributing to a more robust and resilient supply chain. The project will provide critical information to support the continued success of Vermont’s cheese industry and enhance its contribution to the state's overall economic health.

original_description: The U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety Inspection Service (USDA-FSIS) regulatory requirements limits the ability of small food businesses to pursue processing of meat products. The LSU AgCenter's Food Innovation Institute (FOODii) started in 2013 as a food incubator program to help entrepreneurs start small food businesses. At this time, companies are only able to produce food products that are regulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) through the food incubator program. Companies are not able to make any food products that are regulated by the USDA. Currently, FOODii receives several requests per month from entrepreneurs who are interested in making foods that are regulated by USDA-FSIS, many of which are food products that are specific to Louisiana. The purpose of this project is to conduct a feasibility study to determine the technical, operational and financial viability of expanding the current food incubator program to include products that are regulated by USDA-FSIS. This project will benefit LSU AgCenter FOODii and local food manufacturers as it will help to determine the need for a USDA-FSIS inspected facility available for small start-up meat & poultry food businesses.
updated_description: The LSU AgCenter’s Food Innovation Institute (FOODii) has initiated a feasibility study to determine the potential for expanding its current operations to accommodate the processing of meat and poultry products regulated by the USDA-Food Safety Inspection Service. This project will assess the technical and operational requirements, alongside the financial viability, of establishing a facility capable of supporting small start-up food businesses focused on these regulated products. Anticipated outcomes of this study include a clear understanding of the resources needed, such as specialized equipment and operational procedures, to meet USDA-FSIS standards, ultimately leading to the potential development of a dedicated facility. The primary beneficiaries of this project include Louisiana farmers, ranchers, and food processors seeking to scale their operations and expand market access. Furthermore, the project will assist stakeholders within the local food system by addressing a current gap in processing capabilities, allowing for greater production of meat and poultry products. This will improve access to locally produced food for consumers and support the growth of small food businesses within the region. The successful completion of this study will provide a critical roadmap for FOODii and the LSU AgCenter to pursue the development of a facility that directly addresses the needs of food manufacturers operating under USDA-FSIS regulations.

original_description: This project proposes a data-driven approach to strengthen Puerto Rico's local food system. By focusing on new, key buyer categories -- restaurants, chefs, and short term rentals and yacht operators, the project aims to identify and overcome barriers that prevent them from purchasing local produce. Through research, focus groups, and data analysis, the project will pinpoint the specific challenges these buyers face when incorporating local food into their operations. This information will be used to develop a comprehensive marketing plan and targeted media assets designed to address these barriers and promote the benefits of local food acquisition. The project will deliver a report outlining research findings, identified barriers, and opportunities for increased local food sales. It will also produce a data- driven action plan with actionable strategies to mitigate these barriers and encourage local food purchases. Additionally, a targeted marketing plan and marketing materials will be created to support these efforts. The project's success will benefit multiple groups. Local farmers and agricultural producers will gain access to new market opportunities. Consumers will have increased access to fresh, local food. Finally, the target buyer categories themselves will benefit from improved access to high-quality local food options. This project focuses on the planning and development phase. The implementation of the marketing plan falls outside the scope of this project.
updated_description: This project proposes a data-driven approach to strengthen Puerto Rico’s local food system by focusing on new, key buyer categories – restaurants, chefs, and short-term rentals and yacht operators – to identify and overcome barriers preventing them from purchasing local produce. original_description:
This project will increase wholesale and retail direct-to-consumer sales for small-scale farms through collaborative marketing between two member-owned food hubs located on islands in rural Washington. Whidbey Island Grown Cooperative (WIGC) and the San Juan Islands Food Hub (SJIFH) will expand sales opportunities for 67 farmers and 41 value-added producers by 1) revising and implementing a joint marketing plan, 2) designing and purchasing print and social media promotion media, and (3) evaluating the effectiveness of promotion activities.
 
Island farmers and ag producers face barriers in the geographically isolated counties including limited access to markets, and time and knowledge to market their businesses (58% of members are beginning farmers). However, there is significant demand for local products, driven by both community, institutional, and tourist consumers. WIGC and SJIFH provide innovative online marketplaces where producers sell their products through member-owned distribution networks. Using proven strategies from other similarly sized food hubs and USDA Food Hub reports, the project seeks to increase wholesale and retail sales. Shared marketing staff will provide customer service and sales outreach to buyers, create and place marketing materials, recruit and support farmers and ag value-added producers, pilot a food hub to food hub sales and network, and increase management efficiencies to increase the viability of the food hubs and it's members.
updated_description: Whidbey Island Grown Cooperative (WIGC) and the San Juan Islands Food Hub (SJIFH) are undertaking a project to significantly increase wholesale and retail direct-to-consumer sales for small-scale farms and value-added producers within the geographically isolated counties of Washington. This collaborative initiative will focus on expanding sales opportunities for 67 farmers and 41 value-added producers by revising and implementing a joint marketing plan, designing and purchasing print and social media promotional materials, and evaluating the effectiveness of these promotional activities. The project anticipates strengthening the viability of both food hubs and supporting the participating stakeholders, specifically farmers and processors, through increased market access and streamlined operations. WIGC and SJIFH will utilize proven strategies from similarly sized food hubs to achieve these goals, aiming to bolster the overall production capacity and sales volume of the involved agricultural businesses. The anticipated outcomes include a measurable rise in the number of products reaching retail outlets and wholesale buyers, and a more robust and efficient network for the exchange of goods between the two food hubs. These efforts will directly benefit consumers seeking locally produced agricultural products, and bolster the financial stability of the participating farms and producers.

original_description: Arctic Harvest Deliveries is a local food hub in Anchorage, Alaska that aggregates, stores and transports products from over 30 local farmers, ranchers and value added-producers. This project seeks to increase awareness of our online Farm Share program as a convenient way to gain access to these products for individual consumers in communities across Alaska. We will increase marketing efforts to the existing delivery locations of Anchorage, Eagle River, Palmer, Wasilla, Girdwood and Chignik Lagoon Village, as well as to new locations, including Nome, the surrounding Norton Sound villages, and Iguigig. Many of these locations are under served and have low access to fresh produce and local foods.
updated_description: Arctic Harvest Deliveries seeks to increase awareness of its Farm Share program, offering a convenient method for consumers across Alaska to access products sourced from over 30 local farmers, ranchers, and value-added producers. This project will focus on expanding marketing efforts to existing delivery locations in Anchorage, Eagle River, Palmer, Wasilla, Girdwood, and Chignik Lagoon Village, as well as initiating outreach to new locations including Nome and surrounding Norton Sound villages, and Iguigig. The primary goal is to improve access to fresh produce and local food items for a broad range of stakeholders, including farmers, ranchers, and consumers throughout Alaska. Arctic Harvest Deliveries anticipates that this expanded reach will significantly increase the availability of local agricultural products to communities currently experiencing limited access. Ultimately, the project will benefit a wide array of individuals and communities, providing them with greater access to fresh, locally sourced food. The anticipated outcomes include a substantial rise in demand for Farm Share products and a strengthened local food supply chain, supporting the economic viability of local food businesses. This initiative directly impacts communities across Alaska, facilitating the distribution of goods from producers to consumers, and strengthening the connection between food producers and the individuals who consume these products.

original_description:
A persistent need for marketing resources and training has been identified by the state-wide Oregon
Community Food Systems Network (OCFSN) Food Hub working group. This project assesses marketing
opportunities and develops, implements and evaluates a Marketing Plan with training and promotion
for 5 regional food hubs serving 10 Oregon and 2 Washington counties to improve local food sales and
consumption by 10-20% from a 2023 baseline of 1,965 consumers and $908,081. Four of the five hubs
are rural, all serve both low-income/low-access (LI/LA) and non-LI/LA customers, and each is a
member of the OCFSN working group. An Oregon-based Consultant with extensive experience will
conduct the assessment and Marketing Plan with support from hub staff/key partners. Each hub will
have the same media assets purchased with AB testing to determine the effectiveness in rural/urban
and LI/LA or not in 2025 and reassessed and implemented again in 2026 with the same evaluation; a
small portion of funds are provided for non-evaluated media. The Food Hub beneficiaries also benefit
150+ producers, processors and consumers, many of whom are under-served. Outcomes include a final
Marketing Plan with recommendations presented to the Oregon Department of Agriculture, Travel
Oregon and the 19-member Food Hub Working Group who serve approximately 80% of the state to
identify opportunities to leverage resources and engage in the marketing of regional food products.
updated_description: The Oregon Community Food Systems Network (OCFSN) Food Hub working group is undertaking a project to assess marketing opportunities and develop, implement, and evaluate a Marketing Plan for five regional food hubs serving 10 Oregon and 2 Washington counties. This initiative will result in the purchase of standardized media assets, designed to be tested through A/B methodologies to determine their effectiveness in reaching both rural and non-rural populations, as well as low-income and non-low-income consumers. The anticipated outcomes include a finalized Marketing Plan with recommendations presented to the Oregon Department of Agriculture, Travel Oregon, and the 19-member Food Hub Working Group, aiming to identify opportunities for leveraging resources and engaging in the marketing of regional food products. The project directly benefits approximately 150+ farmers, ranchers, processors, and consumers, representing a significant portion of the state’s food system. These stakeholders will gain access to enhanced marketing strategies and increased visibility for their products. The OCFSN Food Hubs will serve as crucial intermediaries in connecting producers with consumers, facilitating the sale of regionally produced agricultural goods. The project’s success will be measured by an estimated 10-20% increase in local food sales and consumption compared to a 2023 baseline of 1,965 consumers and $908,081, and will provide support to the hubs to increase their overall impact.

awardee_name: Northeast Organic Farming Association of New Jersey
original_description:

updated_description: Northeast Organic Farming Association of New Jersey (NOFA NJ) and Jersey Cider Works will undertake a project to identify, analyze, develop, implement, and evaluate innovative marketing opportunities for farm producers in New Jersey and Eastern Pennsylvania utilizing “Farm Winery License Retail Outlets.” This initiative centers around expanding market access for small farmers and processors, specifically focusing on the promotion of shelf-stable and value-added products alongside Jersey Cider Works’ existing offerings within these retail locations. The project aims to support at least ten producers by facilitating productive collaborations and developing targeted marketing plans and physical/digital marketing materials. These materials will be designed to increase sales and enhance the visibility of collaborating producers and retailers within each retail outlet. A key element of the project involves conducting market analyses for each potential retail outlet to ensure optimal product placement and promotional strategies. The anticipated outcome is the creation of a scalable model that can be replicated throughout the Garden State, contributing to increased sales and profitability for participating producers. The primary beneficiaries of this project include small farmers, processors, and the consumers who purchase locally produced goods. Ultimately, NOFA NJ and Jersey Cider Works intend to strengthen the local food system by connecting producers directly with consumers through expanded retail channels and effective marketing strategies.

original_description:
Department of Agriculture, will conduct a research study to better understand the legal barriers experienced by institutional partners and local farmers in Maryland and the Chesapeake region related to increasing participation in Farm to Institution local purchasing programs. Particularly Maryland's Certified Local Farm & Fish Enterprise Program (CLFF), adopted in 2021, that established a goal of 20% (dollar value) local purchasing from regional farms that have a nutrient management plan or from a licensed seafood provider of "certified Chesapeake invasive species". There are currently only 124 eligible CLFF producers and the most recent FY 23 CLFF report reflects that Maryland institutions only sourced a cumulative 0.5% (dollar value) of procured foods from eligible 
CLFF businesses.

This project will use and build upon existing resources to 1) conduct research to identify the specific legal knowledge gaps that exist for regional food producers and institutional buyers, including their food service management companies, like contracting strategies (pricing standards, and procurement processes and regulations) through surveys and focus group meetings with key stakeholders; 2) create opportunities for farmers, institutional buyers, food distribution managers, local agricultural service providers, and community organization members, to learn from each other and establish relationships;
3) design educational materials to bridge identified legal knowledge gaps; and 4) share findings with regional partners and collaborators through a research report, a public Symposium, training workshop template materials, and live webinars.
This project aims to increase technical knowledge about procuring and/or accessing local and regional foods by at least 85 vendors (wholesalers and distributors), 24 school food programs, and 
66 other institutional and farm stakeholders; increase engagement between institutional purchasers and local producers by at least 27 vendors, 12 school food programs, and 15 other stakeholders; 
help facilitate 10 partnerships or collaborations between producers and the local supply network of wholesalers and distributors; and help update the MDA strategic plan for the CLFF Program.
updated_description: The Department of Agriculture will conduct a research study focused on addressing legal barriers faced by regional food producers and institutional buyers within Maryland and the Chesapeake region, specifically concerning the Certified Local Farm & Fish Enterprise Program (CLFF). This project aims to improve participation in local purchasing programs by investigating knowledge gaps related to contracting strategies, procurement processes, and regulations among farmers, food service management companies, and other stakeholders. The Department will support the creation of opportunities for farmers, institutional buyers, distributors, and community organizations to learn from each other and establish relationships. The Department intends to develop educational materials to specifically address these identified legal knowledge gaps and disseminate findings through a research report, a public symposium, and training workshop template materials. Ultimately, the project seeks to increase technical knowledge about procuring and/or accessing local and regional foods by at least 85 wholesalers and distributors, 24 school food programs, and 66 other institutional and farm stakeholders, and to facilitate 10 partnerships or collaborations between producers and the local supply network. The Department anticipates this work will positively impact farmers, ranchers, processors, and other stakeholders seeking to increase their access to local markets and facilitate increased purchasing of regional food products. The Department will deliver these results while helping to update the MDA strategic plan for the CLFF Program.

awardee_name: Board of Regents, NSHE, obo University of Nevada, Reno
original_description: The Desert Farming Initiative is applying on behalf of the Nevada Farm Network to fund a two-year turnkey recruitment and training project, Enhancing Nevada Food Chain Initiatives. DFI will coordinate enhancement actions with partner programs, and facilitate a Leadership Committee made up of local producers and food entrepreneurs to strengthen connections between farmers and the mid-tier value chain. This proposal will leverage and expand on at least four other programs, including the Nevada Small Business Development Centers Made in Nevada e-commerce platform, the Transition to Organic Partnership Program, the Nevada Farm Apprenticeship Program, and the Local Food Network's Nourish and Flourish Non-Profit Commissary Kitchen. The Nevada Farm Network is the first online community of practice for Nevada farmers to access educational resources and make market connections. This project will additionally provide for a pilot project of value-add and processing trainings held at the Local Food Network's kitchen in urban Reno and partner organizations in rural Fallon.
updated_description: The Desert Farming Initiative is seeking funding to implement Enhancing Nevada Food Chain Initiatives, a two-year project designed to strengthen connections within the Nevada agricultural sector. This project will coordinate enhancement actions with multiple partner programs, including the Nevada Small Business Development Centers Made in Nevada e-commerce platform and the Local Food Network’s Nourish and Flourish Non-Profit Commissary Kitchen, to facilitate a Leadership Committee composed of local producers and food entrepreneurs. The initiative will support farmers, ranchers, and processors by expanding access to market connections and promoting the development of regional food businesses. Specifically, the project will leverage existing infrastructure, such as the commissary kitchen in Reno and partner organizations in Fallon, to deliver value-add and processing support. The anticipated outcome is to increase the availability of locally and regionally produced agricultural products through strengthened producer-to-consumer marketing channels. The Desert Farming Initiative aims to support a network of stakeholders engaged in the food chain, creating a more robust and connected agricultural system within Nevada. Ultimately, this project will benefit consumers by increasing the supply of fresh, local food options.

original_description: For more than a decade, the Farm to Institution (F2I) movement in Oregon has made significant strides engaging and coordinating efforts of institutional purchasers, government agencies, nonprofit organizations, and supply chain producers and processors. While successes have helped create lasting change in many institutions, the impact of these resources and partnerships has largely been focused on the Portland Metro Region. While almost 100,000 meals per day are served in institutions in the Portland area, there are more than twice as many meals served in institutions throughout the State. The purpose of this project is to leverage existing proofs of concept in farm to institution (F2I) and take them to scale at a state level.  F2I will be catalyzed in different regions and rural areas of Oregon by establishing the Oregon Farm to Institution Collaborative (OFIC). Project objectives include     Reconfigure the structure of a community of practice focused on F2I   Strengthen regional infrastructure to support F2I projects that improve market channels for producers    Address gaps and barriers identified in F2I work that contribute to inequities in the food system    Develop a shared vision, common language, and purchasing standards for OFIC Key activities to be performed    Design a recruitment strategy grounded in equity and inclusion principles and structure for OFIC   Convene quarterly OFIC meetings  Organize affinity groups, based on institutional setting, regions, and or topics of interest  Hire two value chain coordinators in Oregon   Hold four regional trainings to food service institutions, value chain coordinators, and producers   Complete a land suitability study to determine institutional land for use in F2I projects  Disseminate lessons learned and share impactDeliverables and expected outcomes   Increase in the number of local producers that are connected to institutional market opportunities. By the end of the project, 200 local producers will have gained knowledge about new market opportunities through education and training.   Pilot a farm to hospital project connecting producers to suitable land for food production. By the end of the project, five new or underserved farmers will have institutional land access for farming, and will have support related to food safety certifications and or business plans to meet institutional needs.   Institutions will gain clarity on values based procurement. By the end of the project, 400 institutional partners will be reached through activities and communications from OFIC. Intended beneficiaries  This project will benefit Oregon producers and processors through improved value chain coordination and connections to new institutional markets, thus providing institutions with more options and streamlined processes to purchase local and meet values based purchasing goals. Additionally, the project will benefit communities served by institutions throughout Oregon, like students, patients, and state employees, who will have improved access to healthy, locally grown and produced food.Subrecipient activities     Partner organizations will participate in OFIC and affinity group processes and activities.   Advisors and consultants will provide specific expertise and support, such as  communications strategy, value chain coordination, product development technical assistance, meeting and group facilitation, and topical trainings (ex  food safety, business planning).   Producers will participate in the land suitability study and pilot project, or in other projects and activities of the OFIC.
updated_description: The Oregon Farm to Institution Collaborative (OFIC) project aims to expand farm to institution (F2I) initiatives across Oregon, building upon existing successes in the Portland Metro Region to create a statewide network. This project will focus on establishing key infrastructure elements, including facilitating connections between local producers and institutional purchasing channels, and developing shared standards for procurement. Anticipated outcomes include an increase in the number of farmers and ranchers accessing new market opportunities, with a target of 200 producers gaining knowledge and skills through targeted support. The project will pilot a farm to hospital model, providing five new or existing agricultural producers with access to suitable land for food production, coupled with assistance in meeting institutional food safety requirements and business planning needs. Furthermore, OFIC will reach 400 institutional partners through outreach and communication efforts, enabling institutions to implement values-based procurement strategies. The primary beneficiaries of this project will be Oregon farmers and processors, as well as the communities served by institutions throughout the state, including students, patients, and state employees, who will benefit from increased access to locally produced food. The project will build a collaborative network, strengthening regional food systems and improving the viability of local food economies. This will be achieved through the development of shared standards and the creation of a robust system for connecting producers with institutional demand, ultimately supporting the efficient and reliable supply of fresh, local food.

original_description: The agricultural economic sector in Siskiyou County is facing dire crisis due to persistent drought, year over year wildfires, and environmental pressures faced by small farms. This, paired with major market shifts, is culminating in the urgent decision for small farms across Siskiyou to innovate or exit. Siskiyou Economic Development Council (SEDC) is pairing with key partners throughout Siskiyou and the greater region to launch an initiative to expand market opportunities for Siskiyou producers. These efforts will create opportunities for farms to diversify and create business resiliency in the face of catastrophe.  Connecting Siskiyou s Small Farms and Institutions will establish a critical network of local farms and regional institutional food buyers throughout Siskiyou County and its bordering communities. Through one on one technical assistance, SEDC will work to develop business plans and strategies that will connect key stakeholders and identify gaps in necessary infrastructure to cultivate a thriving farm to institution economy.  This project will provide technical assistance to producers to develop capacity, skill and scale to address the institutional markets and will cultivate a strong foundation for ongoing connections between buyers and small farms. This program will build upon the SEDC s work in the agriculture sector and community food system and will leverage existing relationships with agricultural producers, support organizations, and expert business consultants. This program will strengthen the institutional local food system, identify gaps in infrastructure and supply chain partners, and connect local small farms to viable new markets in an effort to create long term sustainability for one of Siskiyou s most important economic sectors.

original_description: This project invests in strengthening regional, equitable farm to institution (FTI) relationships and value chains in three New England Communities, which in coordination will lead to greater regional and values based food procurement across New England while shifting institutional power dynamics around race. Springfield, MA  New Haven, CT  and Cumberland County, ME will form a Cohort, represented by three community based organizations Springfield Food Policy Council, Cumberland County Food Security Council, City of New Haven Food System Policy Division who are already driving food systems change at the local level. Farm to Institution New England, a regional network backbone organization, will provide project coordination, connect the cohort with regional partners, resources, and trainings, and share stories and strategies developed in each community with the broader network. updated_description: Resilient Relationships, Resilient Supply is a project designed to strengthen Michigan’s Western Lakeshore region’s food system by increasing the sales and consumption of locally grown foods from small and mid-sized producers to schools, early childhood education (ECE) centers, and emergency food providers. original_description: The purpose of the  Implementing a Vibrant, Sustainable, and Equitable Community Food System Across the Arizona Food Systems Network (AZFSN)  RFSP implementation and expansion project is to advance the implementation of the AZFSN Statewide Food Action Plan priorities, goals, objectives, and strategies for action.
